Input: Why do people say they believe science over God when science keeps changing what it says it’s proved and God has not changed? What do you mean that God hasn't changed? He's changed quite a bit over the millennia as the mythology developed. Since you're using capital-G for God, I assume you're referring to the God of the Bible, Yahweh (YHWH). While Yahweh's earliest origins are a bit obscure (and understandably so, since we're talking about something thousands of years ago), the leading idea seems to be the Midianite hypothesis, where Yahweh was originally a god worshipped by the peoples of Midian, the region to the south of Canaan. The early Israelites and Judahites, who were themselves basically just a subset of Canaanite culture at the time, absorbed this god into their pantheon while they still had a polytheistic pantheon. Of course, not all scholars agree with the Midianite hypothesis, and there are plenty of other origins ideas, including that Yahweh was more of a 'home grown' deity within Israel/Judah. On this topic of the earliest origins of Yahweh, the perhaps oldest known records of belief in this particular deity are a couple of inscriptions from Egypt – one from the period of Amenhotep III (14th century BCE), the other from Ramesses II (13th century BCE). In describing a certain group of people, both inscriptions use a phrase translated as something like "The Land of the Shasu yhw" or "Shasu of Yhw". Assuming that Yhw is the same god as YHWH, and that modern ideas of the Shasu being nomads of the region south of Canaan are correct, this seems to support the Midianite hypothesis for Yahweh's origins (though it should be noted, some people think the transfer went the other way around, with the Shasu adopting Yahweh from the Israelites). ABOVE: The inscription describing Shasu of Yhw SOURCE: Shasu - Wikipedia At any rate, no matter how Yahweh first entered the Israelite pantheon, his earliest appearances in Israelite religion were as just one god among many, and not even the most important. I've already discussed Deuteronomy 32:8–9 several times here on Quora, which clearly shows Yahweh as one of the sons of El, receiving Israel as his particular land to rule over, while other sons of El received different lands (more info: Jeff Lewis's answer to Can atheists prove there's no God, since they don't believe in His existence? in Divine Atheist). The earliest writings about Yahweh in the Bible also seem to present him as a storm god and god of war. The New Oxford Annotated Bible is an excellent resource, with very informative essays and copious footnotes from Biblical scholars. They mention this association with a storm god in several footnotes. For example, here was the footnote in reference to 2 Samuel 22:11–16: The LORD is depicted here as the storm God. Cherub (v. 11 ), a mythical, griffin‐like creature. God's voice (v. 14 ) is thunder (Job 40.9; Ps 29.3 ), and he throws lightning bolts at his enemies (v. 15 ). The psalmist envisions the world as flat; he is trapped in the underworld beneath the foundations of the world, which the LORD's roar uncovers (v. 16 ). Other footnotes made reference to "God's storm-cloud chariot" several places, including for Psalm 68:4 ("Who rides upon the clouds, God's storm‐cloud chariot (v. 33; Ps 65.11 )") and for Psalm 65:11 ("Your wagon tracks, God's rain‐cloud chariot."). Personally, reading the Bible on my own, I thought Psalm 77:16–20 was especially in line with those early conceptions of Yahweh as a storm god: When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; the very deep trembled. The clouds poured out water; the skies thundered; your arrows flashed on every side. The crash of your thunder was in the whirlwind; your lightnings lit up the world; the earth trembled and shook. Your way was through the sea, your path, through the mighty waters; yet your footprints were unseen. From those origins, Yahweh went through a transformation within the religion, gradually blending with El to become the primary and most important God of Israel, then through a stage where he was the only God that the Israelites were supposed to worship, though not yet the only god in existence, before the eventual transformation to full monotheism some time around the Babylonian exile. I have another answer where I discussed archaeological finds from during this transition which covers these next two examples in much more detail (Jeff Lewis's answer to Atheists, what are your top 5 reasons for not believing in God and/or Christianity? Please answer with something besides "No proof". in Atheism Now). First is the Mesha Stele, which recounts the same battle as told in 2 Kings 3, but from the point of view of King Mesha of Moab, and is actually older than the Biblical narrative. This stele shows how the Israelites were likely still worshipping more than one god ("the fire-hearth of Daudoh"), and that even their worship of Yahweh hadn't yet been centralized to the Temple of Jerusalem, contradicting the Biblical narrative. The second is the Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions, showing that Yahweh had a wife or consort at the time, the goddess Asherat. And like the Mesha stele, these inscriptions also contradict the Biblical narrative of a centralized worship at the Temple of Jerusalem. And of course, the character of Yahweh continued to develop and change over the generations, including the rise of Rabbinic Judaism after the destruction of the Second Temple, Christianity and it's updates in their scriptures, Islam and their updates, continued revisions in various sects over the years such as the Protestant-Catholic schism, and even more modern updates like Mormons and Jehovah's Witnesses. So in contrast to your implication, Yahweh has changed very much over the generations, from a storm god within a polytheistic pantheon, to the multiple conflicting conceptions of God among modern day Jews, Christians, and Muslims, and all the varying sects within those major branches. God seems to bear all the hallmarks of a mythological character who develops along with the culture of those folks who believe in him. As to the other part of your question, trust in science hardly even deserves a detailed explanation. But just to completely answer your question, here's an excerpt from my self-published book on religion (God? Leaving Christianity | jefflewis.net): One reason to be confident in the scientific process is pragmatic – just look at the results. Science as the formalized discipline that we think of has only been around a few hundred years, getting started in the Renaissance, but not really coming into its own until after the Enlightenment. And look at how fast our technology has progressed in that short time compared to the previous millennia of human existence. We’ve invented telescopes, steam engines, automobiles, semiconductors, airplanes, computers, TVs, radio, lasers, vaccines, antibiotics, cures for some cancers. We’ve sent people to the moon. These accomplishments are all based on knowledge that we’ve learned through science. We wouldn’t have been able to accomplish all of that if we didn’t have an accurate understanding of reality. Granted, there are other fields of science that haven’t yielded practical applications, and possibly never will. The Big Bang may not ever give us any new technologies. But given the technologies we have developed from so many other fields, we know that the methods produce reliable results.

Doubters/non believers/atheists - have you actually read the Bible - how much of the Scripture have you read? Actually, I'm a bit embarrassed to admit that it did take lot of in depth studying of the Bible for me to become an atheist, though I realize that it was mostly because of indoctrination. For example, while I've never read the entirety of the Popol Vuh, from the excerpts I have read, it's clear that it's mythology, and not anything literally true. Same thing with the stories I read from Greek mythology, or what I learned about the ancient Egyptian religion, or plenty of others. I mean, there's nothing wrong with studying those things in depth if they interest you. But for most reasonable people, it only takes is a cursory exposure to realize that those things are cultural products of people, and not divinely true holy scriptures. Now that I've been an atheist for a while, looking at the Bible, it's just as obvious that it fits the same bill, from the just-so aspects of Genesis, to the biased accounts of the historical books, to the frankly absurd premise of the resurrection (God sacrificed himself to himself to save us from himself). So it really is a bit embarrassing to admit that I didn't question it the first time I read the Bible when I was still a Christian. But I justify it by recognizing the indoctrination, the constant reinforcement week after week in Sunday school and church, and then all the social and peer pressure to remain a Christian. But I really am envious of the people who were able to recognize how absurd Christianity is just based on a brief exposure, without all the effort it took for me. So yes. I read the entire Bible once as a Christian. And then about halfway through as an atheist before stalling out. But there really shouldn't be a need for somebody to have to read the entire Bible or study it in depth before realizing that it's just another human created mythology.

Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life? The problem is that this literally isn't possible. The Bible contains many, many contradictions, so you simply can't verify and prove all of the stories. The best you can do is verify some of the stories. And at that point, we're left to cherry pick which stories and lessons we want to say are proven in this hypothetical scenario. Just to go with one example, are we going with the God of Exodus 20:5-6, who threatens "punishing children for the iniquity of parents to the third and the fourth generation," or the God of Ezekiel 18:19-20, who says that "A child shall not suffer for the iniquity of a parent nor a parent suffer for the iniquity of a child; the righteousness of the righteous shall be their own, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be their own"? Because the former seems quite barbaric and not at all worthy of worship. The latter at least seems fair. Still, though, the overall portrayal of God in the Bible is not particularly flattering. You've got the massacre of Noah's Flood with its drowning of infants and children, the horrific treatment of Egyptian commoners and their slaves in the Exodus story (Jeff Lewis's answer to Can you cite the verses of some morality flaws in the Bible?), and then the whole fiery furnace of Hell for the grave sin of doubt. And that's just scratching the surface. So, given all the contradictions within the Bible, even as a hypothetical, you can't imagine a scenario where all of it was proven true. But even going with the overall general portrayal of God in the Bible, he's not a being deserving of worship.

Why is there so much debate over the math question 12÷2(2+4) =? A few other answers have said it's because the expression is ambiguous. But that's not really it. The expression isn't ambiguous at all. As an engineer myself, there's only one way to interpret that expression correctly. No. The issue is that lots of folks' exposure to math doesn't go much if at all beyond the high school level, and simplistic understandings of order of operations like PEMDAS or BODMAS. They don't know any further conventions that affect order of operations. The thing that makes this expression completely unambiguous is that there's no symbol in between the 2 and the parenthesis. That makes it clear that 2(2+4) is a single unit that can't be broken up. So the only appropriate way to interpret this expression is: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) What might have made this expression a bit ambiguous would have been to add a multiplication symbol: 12÷2×(2+4) Then it could be conceivable to interpret it a bit differently, perhaps instead as: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) However, even then, many engineers might interpret it the first way, keeping 2×(2+4) as a single unit as the denominator of the fraction. The reason is that when you're writing math 'inline' as opposed to formatting it the way math should really be written, division symbols are often treated as the fraction bar, with everything to the left assumed to be the numerator, and everything to the right assumed to be the denominator, and not cluttering things up with parentheses. As just one example, here are the definitions of some coefficients from one of my own engineering books, which I can assure you follow the convention that I just described (“my own” is in I own it, not that I wrote it). Really, if you wanted it to be 12/2, you'd probably put the parentheses around that to make it clear that 12/2 was a fraction, and instead write something like: (12/2)(2+4) But just to summarize, the expression as written in the original question isn't ambiguous. The issue is that lots of folks with only limited exposure to math don't know all the conventions affecting order of operations. And if there ever are any questions about ambiguity in an expression you’re writing, don’t be afraid to use parentheses.

Why is the news about the solar eclipse still in the news two days afterwards? Because it was really damn cool, and many of us who saw it are still looking up follow up stories. And considering that those of us who saw it include several high population areas across North America and big cities close enough for people to make day trips out of it (a few million people total traveled to see the eclipse), that’s a lot of potentially interested people. Getting to personally see a total eclipse really is a pretty rare thing, potentially once in a lifetime. Sure, total eclipses happen every year and a half or so, but the path of totality is relatively narrow, and the Earth is pretty big, so most people aren’t all that close to most total eclipses. Getting a total eclipse that passed right over so many major population centers and so close to so many others is going to drive a lot of interest in those locations. How did the dinosaurs evolve into chickens? Let's start with the big dinosaur family tree for some perspective: ABOVE SOURCE: Dinosaur classification - Wikipedia As you can see, birds are a type of theropod dinosaur. They first evolved some time around the middle to late Jurassic. They went through a major bottle neck at the end of the Cretaceous in the mass extinction that wiped out nearly all of the dinosaurs, but a handful of birds managed to survive and carry on the lineage. As far as how birds in particular evolved from non-flying dinosaurs, let's start with a high level diagram from Thomas Holtz's online lecture notes: ABOVE SOURCE: Mesozoic Birds and the Origin of Flight This shows in general the order of appearance of the various characteristics that we now regard as 'birdlike'. It starts way back before even dinosaurs with the hinge-like ankle, and includes traits that evolved over generations, through non-flying dinosaurs, and eventually resulting in modern birds (I intentionally didn't say 'culminating', because who knows what's in store for bird evolution in the future.) Here's another diagram from Dr. Holtz. This one focuses a bit tighter on the emergence of birds. They evolved out of the specific theropods known as eumaniraptora. ABOVE SOURCE: Rise of the Birds If you loosely count all Avialae as birds, their closest cousins were the deinonychosaurs, which looked an awful lot like birds, but couldn't fly. Between these two diagrams, they illustrate that many traits that we now associate with birds evolved for ground-based animals, and so must have served purposes that had nothing to do with flight. This includes feathers. More primitive down-like feathers were probably just for insulation, while more complex feathers might have evolved for display. Deinonychosaurs even had 'wing' feathers, despite their arms not being wings, so even these feathers had some other purpose – perhaps as a way to flap to help boost their running abilities, or maybe as a way to help them 'parachute' from long drops, or maybe something else. But obviously, with such feathers evolving before birds, flight couldn't have been their original purpose. I don't know as much about chicken evolution in particular. But chickens are domesticated animals, and their wild ancestors were red junglefowl. This is a species of bird that spends a lot of its time foraging on the ground, but which can still fly when the need arises. ABOVE SOURCE: Reddit ABOVE SOURCE: Red Junglefowl in flight - Bird Ecology Study Group Jungle fowl are part of a larger group that includes pheasants, partridges, turkeys, and peacocks. Here's a larger family tree of birds to show where they fit in (the Galliformes): ABOVE SOURCE: Evolutionary Radiation of Birds So that's the quick story. A lot of 'bird like' traits had already evolved in non-flying dinosaurs, such as feathers, being warm blooded, their air sac respiratory system, etc. Then, one particular branch of dinosaurs, the birds, evolved the ability to fly, and began diversifying from there. There was a major bottleneck when most species of birds were wiped out at the end of the Cretaceous, which wiped out a lot of the then existing variation (like many birds still having teeth), but the survivors went on to diversify into all the birds we have today, including chickens. Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool? For just about any question that starts with, "Why has Quora...", the answer is almost always money. I didn't get started on Quora back at the very beginning, but I still got on early enough to get a taste of what it was at its best. I mean, you still got people like Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton contributing answers when I first started using the site. But as great as Quora was back then, it was operating at a loss. It was living off of the cash from investors, trying to build up its userbase and reputation so that it would eventually become profitable. Those investors weren't putting their money into Quora just for fun. They want to see a return on their investment. And operating a social media site is expensive. Googling it just now, it has something like 400 million active monthly users. That takes tons of hardware and bandwidth, which costs tons of money. So, if Quora wants to start turning a profit, they have to find ways to reduce costs and increase the things that bring in money. And bringing in money mostly boils down to advertising, which means getting people to 'engage' with the platform. So, the questions Quora's management asks aren't how changes will affect the user experience, but how they'll affect the bottom line. And cutting down on moderation is an easy way to cut costs. Can a negative user experience drive some people away from the site? Sure. But you're still here asking questions, and I'm still here answering them. And according to Semrush.com, it looks like Quora's traffic has just continued growing over the past 6 months, despite all of us users complaining about the decline in the user experience (accessing stats going beyond 6 months cost money that I'm not going to spend just to answer this question): In short, the user experience on Quora has declined because it saves Quora money by not having to pay as much for moderation, while it doesn’t seem to have had a big impact on the engagement which brings in the ad revenue.

Why are there still altruists evolutionarily? I hate to say it, but the other answers to this question, even from folks who normally write good stuff, are wrong, misleading, or fudging the definition of altruism. True altruism goes beyond mere cooperation or being helpful. It means being helpful without any benefit to yourself, or from an evolutionary perspective, at least a benefit to your own genes. And natural selection is never going to favor such behaviors of pure altruism. To the extent that altruism does happen and has an evolutionary origin, it's because evolution is a mindless process without perfect aim, and some behaviors are missing their target. To begin with, there's the concept of kin selection. What's really important to evolution is increasing the copies of your genes. When parents help their direct offspring, nobody refers to that as 'altruism', since the offspring share half of the genes from each parent, so it's obvious that the parents are protecting their own genetic legacy. But you share genes with more relatives than just your own children. As the famed biologist JBS Haldane supposedly once quipped, "I would gladly give up my life for two brothers or eight cousins." Promoting your own genes by helping relatives is not altruism, at least in an evolutionary sense. Cooperation beyond relatives can also be favored by natural selection, but that's because cooperation brings benefits to all parties involved, so it's not really altruism, either. This can even cross species boundaries, such as the textbook example of cleaning stations in coral reefs, where cleaner fish and shrimp will pick the dead skin and parasites off of larger fish, even fish that could easily eat them if they tried. The cleaners get a meal, while the cleanees get improved hygiene. Everyone benefits from this cooperation (well, everyone but the parasites). One of the other answers to this question used the example of helping an injured member of your tribe to recover, so that they can once again become productive and contribute to your tribe in the future. Well, that's the ulterior motive right there – their future contributions. Going even further, in complex social groups like we humans form, individuals benefit immensely from being a part of the tribe, but everybody also has a vested interest in keeping out freeloaders and cheats. So public displays of charity help to increase your social capital, showing that you are a valuable, contributing member of the tribe, which will provide you with indirect benefits down the road. So even public displays of charity aren't altruistic in these conditions. (I’m not saying people are so conniving in their motivations, but why evolution would have instilled such instincts in us.) The tribalism that's so common in human societies helps to show that these behaviors really are for the benefit of the individual, and not altruism. From a selfish perspective, it makes sense to help out those in your own tribe, since they're more likely to be family in the first place (kin selection), or folks who will be able to help you out in the future (long term cooperation). People are much, much less charitable to non-relatives, or to those outside their own tribe (the other). But like I said way up in the beginning, evolution doesn't have perfect aim. It's not a conscious creator who implements designs the same way an intelligent designer might. Evolution often results in good enough, not perfection. So a general instinct to help those in your own tribe will be helpful, but could spill over into helping strangers. Parental instincts to help your own children and those of your near relatives can spill over into helping babies in general. And of course, in the more intelligent animals like us apes, dolphins & whales, some birds, and a few others, our extremely complex personalities provide even more opportunities for individuals to consciously choose actions that may not be in their evolutionary best interests. It doesn't mean natural selection favors those choices, but rather that natural selection does favor the larger set of complex behaviors, because their benefits outweigh the occasional 'poor' choice (poor in an evolutionary sense, not necessarily in a moral one). Finding examples of true altruism that weren't just the occasional misfiring of otherwise evolutionarily beneficial behaviors would actually be a major blow to our current understanding of evolution. Outside the somewhat controversial theories of group selection, there's no mechanism to explain why an organism would help out another organism if it didn't gain at least some benefit for itself or its genes. But cooperation, tit-for-tat, kin selection, and complex behaviors in intelligent animals do all go to show that the alternative isn’t a cut-throat, dog eat dog world. There are still plenty of reasons evolution will favor cooperation, since cooperation can bring benefits to everybody.

Can a Republican ever win the presidency again without some kind of a reset? Anyone remember headlines like these from 2008, when Obama had a strong victory and Democrats won a majority in the House and a supermajority in the Senate? Well, it only took until 2010 for the Republicans to win back control of the House, which they held onto for 8 more years until the 2018 election. And while Obama did manage to win re-election in 2012, I think we all remember what happened in 2016. And even in 2020, Trump only lost thanks to about 40 thousand voters in 3 key swing states. Even this year, 538 is currently giving Trump a 40% chance of winning the election, which is barely worse than a coin toss. That's just the nature of our two party system and polarized politics. The Democratic and Republican candidates will always get roughly half the vote. And with the way the electoral college currently biases the results towards rural states that tend to favor Republicans, presidential elections in particular will remain competitive, even when Democrats might have a nationwide advantage in raw numbers. So yes, the Republicans still have a very good chance of winning the presidency even maintaining their current strategies. They have a very good chance of winning this year. So don't get complacent like 2016, thinking a Democratic victory is a sure thing. Everybody needs to get out and vote to make sure their voice is heard.

If you could only eat meat or be vegetarian for the rest of your life, which one would you choose? That's not a tough decision at all, especially as the question is only specifying a vegetarian diet, and not the more extreme vegan diet. I already eat plenty of meals that count as vegetarian. I don't eat any meals that consist solely of meat. Just this morning, I had dippy eggs with toast and a bit of jalapeño jelly (dippy eggs as in the Pennsylvania version, not the UK version). I've actually switched over to getting the falafel gyro instead of lamb at the local gyro shop. I tend to go for veggie toppings on my pizza. I love bread, brownies, and other baked foods. It's tough to imagine a world without dairy products (because milk is not meat). And most important of all, is a life without potatoes even a life worth living? ABOVE: Just a small sampling of the dishes you can make with potatoes – and that image doesn’t even have any fries, chips, or good old fashioned mashed potatoes. SOURCE: 15 Things to Make with a Bag of Potatoes - What To Make With A Lot of Potatoes Don't get me wrong. In the real world where I don't have to make this choice, I'll go on enjoying a balanced diet of all different types of food. But if I had to choose between meat and potatoes, the potatoes are the clear winner.

For those who experienced the eclipse today, what are your thoughts? I've seen a few sources overhyping eclipses a bit, so I don't want to oversell it, but it was very, very cool. Living about 2 hrs outside the path of totality myself, it was definitely worth the trip to get myself into a location to see the total eclipse, since a total solar eclipse really is an altogether different experience than a partial solar eclipse. Since my wife is working a contract away from home right now and got a few days off, we decided to make an event of it. We both arrived in Ft. Worth the day before, and spent the day going to a small wine tasting festival and then a night out in downtown Ft. Worth (hat tip to The Flying Saucer). The next morning, the day of the eclipse, we drove down to Mansfield, a small town on the outskirts of the DFW metro area, since that's where most of my wife's family lives. There's nothing like last minute planning, so an hour before the eclipse was forecast to start, we were at Walmart buying hotdogs, hamburgers, and other supplies for a cookout, while my sister in law was scrambling to clean up her house. I did plan enough ahead to have my telescope ready to go, along with a sun funnel that I threw together on Saturday. I got that set up in her driveway as family members began rolling in, so we were able to track the eclipse with that, while everybody had their own eclipse glasses, too. Our eclipse watching group included a few of us who had the day off, one person who called in to take the day off, and a few nieces and nephews skipping the school day (worth it). ABOVE: The start of the eclipse through my telescope – note that this setup lets you see the sunspots, which you don't notice through eclipse glasses. Our biggest stressor was the weather. The forecast was for a cloudy day, and the day of did turn out to be partly cloudy. Throughout the time that the eclipse was occurring, we'd have clouds periodically roll in and block our view. There was one particularly big one that rolled into place as totality was getting close. Google told me that totality was supposed to start at 1:39 in Dallas, and I don't think that cloud blew out of the way until 1:36. So it cleared out just in time. Though I do feel sorry for the people downwind of us who had that cloud blow in just in time to block their view. When the sun was completely blocked by the moon, it really was awesome. I haven't seen many photos that do justice to what it looks like with your own eyes. This photo below is about as close as I've seen, though it was from a previous eclipse back in 2010. Per the description at the site where I found this, it's a composite image composed of short, medium, and long exposures. Compared to yesterday's eclipse, the below photo is missing a couple solar flares that we could just barely see as red spots along the edge of the moon. But this photo does give a sense of the wispy arms of the corona stretching out from the Sun. ABOVE CREDIT: Dennis Di Cicco ABOVE SOURCE: Basic Solar Eclipse Info — Great American Eclipse You've probably seen umpteen million descriptions of eclipses by now, but yes, it really did get dark and noticeably cooler during totality (it actually started cooling down before the Sun was completely blocked). It wasn't quite as dark as night, but more like the mid stages of dusk and dawn. We could make out a couple planets (Venus and Jupiter, I think), though not really any stars. We didn't have a great view of the horizon, and we were all focused on the eclipse itself, anyway, so I didn't notice the 360° sunset that others have mentioned. And I didn't notice any animals doing anything strange, either (though a flock of birds did fly overhead right as totality happened, which was pretty cool). One thing that seems obvious in hindsight is that I should have used sunscreen. Even partially blocked by the moon, staring at the Sun for a couple hours is still a lot of sunlight. A few of us ended up with a bit of a sunburn. Now, to address the overhyping, I've heard some people describe the eclipse as an almost spiritual or transcendent experience. Even Randall Munroe of XKCD fame said "A total eclipse is like someone broke the sky." Yeah, that's going too far. It's a very cool thing to see, but it's not life changing. If there's going to be an eclipse reasonably close by, or if you've got enough money to travel, it's worth seeing a total eclipse at least once in your life. I'd already seen multiple partial eclipses (including an annular eclipse just last year), and they simply don't compare to a total eclipse. But keep your expectations grounded in the fact that all it really means is that you're in a big shadow. A shadow cast by the Moon, but still just a shadow. ETA: I nearly forgot to mention, we also had an assortment of appropriately themed snacks. I had a hard time finding the Moon Pies, so I suspect we were far from the only people who did this.

Why would anyone buy a hamburger at McDonald's when there are other hamburger places with better quality hamburgers at the same or lower prices? I challenge your premise. Let's go with prices, first. Here are the prices of fast food cheeseburgers at the fast food places I go to most often for burgers*, in my order of preference. I listed the bacon cheeseburgers at the other places, because while I get a plain cheeseburger at McDonald's, I usually go for the bacon cheeseburger at the other places (with the McDonald's cheeseburger being so minimalist with toppings, the salt in the patty and pickles is plenty, whereas the other burgers need the bacon to balance the lettuce and tomato). McDonald's has by far the cheapest cheeseburger. Granted, it's also the smallest. But it's still plenty of calories for a normal lunch. And if I'm extra hungry, I can get two, and it would still be cheaper than the other options. As far as flavor, McDonald's is my favorite out of the fast food places. There's just something about the McDonald's burger that hits just right, the perfect combination of those minimalist ingredients. I've said this before, but the other fast food places are trying to be like something I'd make on the backyard grill, and often not quite succeeding, while McDonald's is just doing its own thing. If I'm in the mood for a bunch of toppings, I might go to one of those other places (Whataburger is great at 2 am). But when I'm in the mood for a McDonald's cheeseburger, nothing else really matches it. If I've got a bit more time to sit down instead of going through a drive through, then I've got more options besides fast food. A local place called Pat's Drive In is probably my favorite restaurant burger in town ($4.79 for a cheeseburger), followed by a very small chain, Bricktown Brewery ($10.50 for a burger, but fries are included – and I can get a beer to go with it). So, out of fast food places, McDonald's does have my favorite burger, and it's the cheapest, to boot. It makes it the obvious choice when I'm in the mood for a fast food burger. *When I go to other fast food places, I tend to get chicken sandwiches, not burgers. e.g. Jack in the Box, Wendy's, etc. And since I live in a small town, we don't have some of the other national chains (though I've found a few of those to be overrated when I have tried them while traveling, e.g. In-n-Out – their burgers are fine, but their fries kinda suck). 👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? I guess there are two shades of meaning to this question. Why did people write about Jesus at all (which I'll cover first). And why did so many people write about him in particular, to the relative exclusion of similar cult leaders at the time (which I'll get to a bit later). Broadly speaking, people were motivated to write about Jesus for the same reasons that they write about anybody. I've discussed a more modern day cult leader here on Quora before, Sathya Sai Baba*. He just died relatively recently in 2011, and you can find a ton of stuff written about him by his followers, from an official biography, to innumerable online essays by rank and file followers. You can even find answers by many of his followers right here on Quora (just type his name into the Quora search bar). Whatever you might think of his own motivations (e.g. were his 'miracles' intentional sleight of hand deception), he struck a chord with people and was able to parlay that into fame and a successful movement in his lifetime. Will Sai Baba's cult survive for centuries like Jesus's did? Who knows? Some sects seem to die out with the death of their leader, while others seem to resonate even afterwards. There are plenty of examples of this persistence, from major religions right down to smaller sects – Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Mormons, Seventh-day Adventists, Rastafarianism, Scientology, etc. I don't think there's really any way of knowing why Jesus's cult became so hugely popular compared to all the other similar cults in that time and place. Heck, history has relegated John the Baptist to basically supporting cast in the Jesus story, despite being a leader of a religious movement in his own right.** There have actually been studies on smaller scale versions of this. Back in 2003, some researchers created a music download website that they could control to run experiments. They tested a specific set of songs across multiple groups. None of the groups could see what songs the other groups had downloaded or how the other groups rated all of the songs. So in each group, there was equal opportunity for any song to go 'viral'. And what they found that was it was probabilistic and random at the same time (stochastic). Some songs tended to end up in the top downloads more often, while other songs tended to remain relegated to the bottom, but the specific songs that became the most popular varied from group to group with no way to definitively predict it ahead of time. It seemed to come down to random chance and extreme sensitivity to initial conditions. Here’s a pop-sci article discussing the study, and the actual research report: So, there probably was something to Jesus's message about loving your neighbor, caring for the poor, and not being judgmental that resonated with people. But why that particular cult ended up becoming a major world religion as opposed to the similar cults is probably down to chance. Had history played out a bit differently, billions of people might now be worshipping John the Baptist, wearing necklaces with dinner platters instead of crucifixes. * That previous answer about Sathya Sai Baba can be found here: ** It’s interested to read Josephus’s mention of John the Baptist, where he describes John the Baptist as an important figure in his own right, not some second fiddle to Jesus like in the Gospels:

If you have a Bible at hand, can you open it up to a random page and see what it says? Maybe it will change your life. Okay. I decided to give this a try, and I really did open up to random pages rather than cherry picking verses that I knew were problematic just to make a point. And to up the odds that I’d get something good, I actually tried it three times, not just once. Here’s what I got: First Attempt – Joshua 14 and Joshua 15 Well, there's nothing really profound or life changing here. It was mostly just details of how the conquered areas of the Promised Land were divied out to the various Jewish people. Just to give a taste of how tedious it is: And their south boundary ran from the end of the Dead Sea, from the bay that faces southward; it goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, makes a turn to Karka, passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Wadi of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary. If you wanted to be less charitable, you could point out that the Israelites were the evil conquerors who went in and subjugated or displaced the people already living there, but that kind of thing is so common throughout history that it's just par for the course. I mean, look at how many times the lands that would become England were invaded and conquered by outsiders, or basically the entire history of Rome. (Also, somewhat thankfully, these stories about conquering the Promised Land probably aren’t true – Frans du Plessis's answer to Do we have extra-biblical evidence for the origins of the Israelites?) Second Attempt – 2 Chronicles 1 and 2 Chronicles 2 Well, at least we get one of the classic Bible stories, here, with God offering Solomon anything he wanted, and Solomon asking for wisdom. But it all reads as just typical ancient literature, so still nothing life changing. I'll note the the final couple verses, though: Then Solomon took a census of all the aliens who were residing in the land of Israel, after the census that his father David had taken, and there were found to be one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred. Seventy thousand of them he assigned as laborers, eighty thousand as stonecutters in the hill country, and three thousand six hundred as overseers to make the people work. Huh. No calls to send them back across the border where they came from, or complaints that the immigrants were stealing Israelite jobs. Just a pragmatic approach of putting them to work. I feel like there might be a lesson there for certain modern day folks who claim to follow the Bible. Third Attempt – Job 30 and Job 31 These were the chapters where Job wrapped up his defense to his friends who insisted that he must have done something wrong to have incurred God's wrath, while Job insisted that he'd done nothing wrong and had lived a good life. It's really just a reminder of how unfair and cruel God can be. As I've said elsewhere, the lesson one takes away from Job is that might makes right, and God is the mightiest of all. So I actually gave it three shots. None of the chapters I came across offered anything particularly profound or life changing. And actually, that is an important point that I don't think a lot of folks really understand. You so often hear people say that, even if you're not religious, at least the Bible is great literature, or carries profound moral lessons. But on the whole, it isn't, really. There may be certain sections of the Bible that are good (e.g. Ecclesiastes). But when you look at the entire Bible, it's a very mixed bag, with the tedious and mundane parts outnumbering the good parts.

Having a new species require at least 2 mutated species (male and female) with same characteristics, and they need to be around the same area to have any chance of mating. If it is that difficult, how are there so many species on earth today? What you're referring to is saltationism (from the Latin term for jump), sometimes referred to a little more colorfully as the hopeful monster hypothesis. The idea was that large macromutations create new species in a single blow. But, as the colorful name and your question point out, how would such hopeful monsters find partners to mate with? This idea did have some proponents back in the late 1800s and early 1900s, but the incorporation of genetics into evolutionary theory and the Modern Synthesis caused the idea to be mostly abandoned, at least for sexually reproducing animals. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. Populations already have genetic diversity. It's why no two individuals look exactly alike. And genetic mutation is decently common. In us humans, for example, it seems that pretty much everybody has a handful of new mutations*. But this genetic diversity doesn't keep us (or other populations of animals) from mating. And the new mutations that do creep into the population don't instantly create new species. They just add to the existing genetic diversity. For a population to split into two species takes time and isolation. The population somehow gets split into two separate populations, let's say Population A and Population B, that can't or don't mate with each other. These constant mutations will continue to spontaneously arise in each population, but they'll be limited to their respective populations. Mutations that arise in Population A, for example, can mix into that population over generations as all those animals mate with each other, but as long as Population B remains isolated from Population A, those mutations won't jump over to Population B. They'll be limited to Population A. And the same goes vice versa for new mutations that arise in Population B. Over time, as each of these population acquires more and more different mutations, they'll become more and more distinct from each other. Eventually, they'll have become different enough to be new species, but it's still a gradual process, with no stark dividing line. ABOVE SOURCE: Islands of speciation and speciation on islands This also explains why species is such a fuzzy boundary, with 'lumpers' and 'splitters' often disagreeing on whether different populations should be separate species, or merely subspecies. For example, a single study from 2020 , showed that there could be anywhere from 2 to 6 different species of giraffe depending on which specific criteria you used to define species. But sexually reproducing animals aren't the only organisms out there. Many types of animals are hermaphrodites, with male and female reproductive organs on the same individual. Many plants also produce male and female reproductive organs (stamens and pistils) on the same plant. If one of these types of organisms were to experience a substantial mutation, then it could potentially create a new species with that individual. In fact, this actually has been observed decently often for plants (take a look at section 5.1 of this page, Observed Instances of Speciation). Another exception is animals that reproduce by parthenogenesis, which is just a fancy term to describe animals where an egg can develop without being fertilized by a male. A notable recent case is the marbled crayfish. Their ancestral species is the slough crayfish from Georgia and Florida. People captured slough crayfish for pets, which led to captive breeding to supply the pet trade. Some time around the mid '90s, somebody in Germany discovered the new species, marbled crayfish, which can reproduce parthenogenetically. This new species like arose from a mutation in a single individual. (You might also see these animals referred to by their German name, marmokrebs.) So, your intuition was partially right about sexually reproducing animals. Even if there were massive mutations that would create a new species in a single individual, the odds of such mutations happening simultaneously to create a male and female of that new species are so astronomically low as to be effectively impossible. But, that’s not the way speciation actually occurs in sexually reproducing animals. It’s a gradual process among populations due the accumulation of many, many mutations. But among other types of organisms that can reproduce by themselves and so don’t have the problem of being hopeful monsters, then speciation can sometimes happen in a single individual. * The overall mutation rate is on the order of 100 - 200 mutations per person. But given that something like 90% of our genome is junk DNA, most of those mutations don't do much at all. Still, it seems that we do all get at least a handful of mutations to functional DNA. What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary? First off, this question hits one of my pet peeves – using the word 'necessary' without any context, implying that 'necessary' is some intrinsic property all on its own. It isn't. Just about every time this word is used, it's in relation to a specific outcome. For example, are fermentable sugar and yeast necessary ingredients? Yes if you're making beer or bread. Not so much if you're grilling a steak. Considering that TV itself isn't a necessity, hardly anything around the medium is necessary in any universal sense. It all depends on what outcomes you want. So, if you're asking if these disclaimers are necessary – necessary for what? If you wanted to be cynical, you could say that the purpose of these disclaimers is merely a way to silence the busybodies with a token message that only lasts a few seconds, that most viewers will forget about almost as soon as the action starts. The network can still show controversial or 'problematic' content essentially unaltered, retaining most of the audience that enjoys those shows (and their associated advertising dollars). The networks have balanced the conflicting influences of alienating more politically correct viewers to losing more old fashioned viewers, and figured these disclaimers were the best compromise. It's the free market at work. If you want to be more charitable about their motivations, such disclaimers do play at least a small part in consciousness raising. It may only be a short message, but at least it's putting it in people's heads that these depictions may not be so benign. And so when they do watch these shows, they're not just uncritically accepting such depictions as right or normal. I think this is especially true when it comes to kids watching TV. I know, some folks like to say that parents should be aware of all the media their children are consuming. That's a bit unrealistic, not to mention a bit questionable advice in its own right. Such constant supervision has taken on its own derogatory term these days – helicopter parenting. On the other extreme, you have folks fondly remembering the 'good old days', when kids roamed their neighborhoods unsupervised for hours on end (and believe me, even back then, we found parents' stashes of 'questionable' media hidden in boxes in the attic). Ideal parenting is somewhere in between – a balance of oversight and child independence, where parents have a general idea of what their kids are up to, but not necessarily screening each and every TV show their kids are going to watch. And in this context, such disclaimers are important in the consciousness raising of children, who don't have the background and experience to fully understand such shows like adults. So yes. I think these disclaimers serve a purpose. They help in the consciousness raising of both nostalgic older viewers and younger first time viewers. And considering that it's such a short message and that the shows themselves are unaltered, it seems that it's only the most easily offended who get worked up about these disclaimers, anyway.

If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work? It's not fiction in the same sense as a novel, where one person sat down to write a story. Much of what ended up in the Bible were legends and stories that had been floating around in that culture for generations, spread largely by word of mouth and oral history. Sure, every once in a while some scribe might have written down a particular version of one of the legends, but these wouldn't have initially taken on the authority of 'scripture', and the legends would continue to develop within the larger society. As a more modern day example, consider Grimm's Fairy Tales. The Brothers Grimm didn't invent these stories themselves. They went around collecting stories from German folklore. You can see this in the books now referred to as the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy). By using critical analysis to study these books, it's clear that they were the result of combining four prior traditions, now known as the Yahwist, Elohist, Priestly, and Deuteronomist sources, with a round of editing by a person or group known as the Redactor. As just one example from the Old Testament, the Noah's Ark story can trace its origins back to older Sumerian flood myths such as Gilgamesh and Atrahasis. And even the story within Genesis is an intertwining of the Priestly and Yahwist traditions, with conflicting details throughout the story, such as the number of animals to take aboard (one pair of each kind vs. seven pairs of the clean kinds), how long the flood lasted (40 days in the Yahwist source per Genesis 7:17 vs. 150 days in the Priestly source per Genesis 7:24), and twice repeating that Noah went into the ark (7:7-9 and again at 7:13-16). The New Testament development was a bit more rapid, but it was still the result of stories being passed along by word of mouth for decades before a few educated converts to Christianity decided to write them down. Some of those accounts eventually acquired enough of a reputation to be included in the official canon, but many more never acquired the status of 'scriptures', and are regarded as merely early Christian writing. Basically, it's the same as many other mythologies. Nobody necessarily sits down with the intent to create a story from scratch. It's stories that get passed on orally from generation to generation, that develop and morph over the years. Some scribes write down the stories from time to time, and the written versions that strike a chord become canonical.

Why does my keyboard have a caps lock key? It must have some purpose, right? This is a good question. Is there really a need for a caps lock key on modern keyboards? How many times do most people use it intentionally, vs. eNDING UP WITH SENTENCES UNINTENTIONALLY WRITTEN IN ALL CAPS? The obvious function is that it lets you write in all caps, LIKE THIS, without having to hold down the shift key. This stems from old, mechanical typewriters, where the shift key actually did mechanically shift the typing mechanism to switch between lower case and upper case letters, which required a decent amount of force on the key. So, for prolonged all caps typing, a shift-lock locked the mechanism in the shifted position, easing the load on your pinky fingers. But shift-lock shifted all the keys, including the symbols on numbers, so a slightly later innovation was caps-lock that only shifted the letters, not the entire keyboard. Once electric typewriters, word processors, and early computers came around, the effort to hold down shift wasn’t nearly so hard, but it was still nice to have a caps-lock key. Remember that typewriters and early printers (like Daisy wheels) still didn’t allow for much formatting or different font sizes, so all-caps was still a convenient way to distinguish things like titles and headings. But on modern day computers? Just about any serious project that needs to be in all-caps can be handled by software, and in many cases, it’s even preferable to do it that way. For example, for headings in a paper, you should type them out in normal mixed case, e.g. Heading Example. Then, if you want it in all caps, just change the heading style to all caps, and the word processing software will take care of it for you. But if you decide later to switch back to mixed case, it’s just a quick change of the style rather than re-typing everything. In my own field, technical drawings use all caps as the standard for drawing annotations, but this can also be handled through software settings instead of using caps-lock (e.g. Displaying Annotation Notes in Uppercase). Even typing here on Quora, there are already a basic text formatting options. Adding an all-caps to that would be simple. There may be some niche applications, like programming, where caps-lock still has a bit of use, but I imagine a lot of that’s driven by complacency. Remove the caps-lock key from the keyboard, and programming software would pretty quickly include software features*. The more I think about it, the more I’d like to see the caps-lock key done away with, to free up that space on the keyboard for something more useful. Maybe replace it with a keyboard shortcut to enable all caps (like alt-shift-c), or at least relegate it to a far corner of the keyboard where you’re less likely to hit it by accident. Here’s something related I found doing a bit of googling: *I’m only a novice programmer, with most of my experience in Visual Basic (which just earned me several snorts of derision from the real programmers). But even back in VB 6, I only worried about capitalization when I declared my variables. After that, I typed them in all lower case, and VB would automatically convert them to the capitalization from when they were declared. Not only did it save me the effort of pressing the shift key, it was a nice, quick double check that I typed in the correct variable name (if it didn’t update capitalization, I’d made a typo).

How is it possible that if I have an addiction, the law allows my children to be stolen and kept away from me and then I have to pay child support? Children aren’t property. You don’t own them. They are citizens in their own right, with an expectation of protection from the state. Parents have an obligation and a civic responsibility to raise children properly. If they can’t meet that responsibility, or (not necessarily in your case) perform actions like abuse in outright opposition to that responsibility, then it’s the state’s responsibility to step in and protect those young citizens. And of course, biological parents are still obligated to pay child support since it was their actions that brought these children into the world. Otherwise, I wish you well in your recovery, and that you may be reunited with your children, or at least be able to form a healthy relationship with them. Of course, once they’re old enough to have a say in the matter, their feelings about a relationship would need to be reciprocal.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? Yes. And Trump could beat Harris. Presidential elections in the past 30 years have all been relatively close. Roughly half the votes will go to either candidate, plus or minus a few percent that decides who will win (and a few more percent to third party candidates). And of course, that whole process gets filtered through the electoral college, so a candidate doesn't even need a majority of the popular vote to win the election. ABOVE SOURCE: United States presidential election - Wikipedia This year will be no different. Trump will get around half the vote. Harris will get around half the vote. Whoever performs best in the swing states will win the overall election. Sure, you've got plenty of people right now making 'guarantees' about who will win. And given that it's really a binary choice, a lot of those people will inevitably end up picking the eventual winner. But it doesn't mean they actually had any better insight than the rest of us. It means they just got lucky by calling the coin toss. I think we can safely predict, at least, that Robert Kennedy is not going to win. Side note: I don't mean to discount polling as worthless. I think it still is useful and valid as long as you understand it's limitations. It's just that polling can't tell you much when elections are decided by less than the polling margin of error. Another side note: This question is from 2016, but for obvious reasons, it's taken on a new found relevance.

And the restaurant itself was a weird vibe of run down yet festive. Anyway, here are a few photos to try to give a sense of the place: ABOVE SOURCE: Google Maps ABOVE SOURCE: Rainbow Fountain photos ABOVE SOURCE: Rainbow Fountain photos ABOVE SOURCE: Rainbow Fountain photos But the food? ABOVE SOURCE: Rainbow Fountain photos Oh man, those tortas were delicious. Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? I don't see any 'holes', per se. It just doesn't seem practical for any real world purposes. If I understand the description in the question, you'll end up with something like this on your sub: You've got a tank big enough to allow 1 gallon of sea water to drive a turbine to generate power, and that power will be used for electrolysis to create hydrogen and oxygen. Pressure can be thought of as energy per volume: So, just rearranging a bit, energy is pressure times volume. You need some type of pressure differential to get any work out of that, which is why the contraption has that tank at atmospheric pressure in the diagram above. But since atmosphere pressure is so much lower than the water pressure that deep, we can just assume it's negligible. Anyway, assuming everything was 100% efficient (which it won't be), using the correct value of 16k psi for the pressure in the deepest part of the ocean, and that I’ve done all my math properly, that 1 gallon of water has a potential energy of 308k ft-lb or 0.156 hp-hr, or in terms more familiar to folks who aren't U.S. based engineers, 418 kJ or 116 Wh. In contrast, a AA battery has roughly 3.9 Wh. So your device, at most, has the potential to generate as much energy as 30 AA batteries. In actuality, after all of the efficiencies are accounted for, it will be even less than that. I think your sub is going to need more than 30 AA batteries worth of energy to complete its mission, so you're spending more energy to perform this mission than what you get out of it. So, while this device could theoretically generate hydrogen in principle, there are far more practical ways of generating power.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I've met intelligent creationists, but never any creationists in person who actually understood evolution. Every time I talked to an intelligent creationist about how they thought evolution worked, I invariably found that they didn't actually understand. Their views tend to be a mish-mash of Lamarckism, teleological thinking, evolution being progression towards a goal, and human exceptionalism, along with a lack of knowledge of how evolution works, and even a lack of knowledge of modern day organisms. These types of misconceptions drive such questions as wondering why there are still monkeys if we evolved from monkeys (though it's never why there are still birds if penguins evolved from birds), or wondering whether the first fish to crawl onto land would have had either gills or lungs (totally ignoring all the existing fish that have both). You can browse through the Index to Creationist Claims to get an idea of the types of arguments creationists might use. I don't wholly blame these folks, either. They were raised in an environment where creationism was the default, from their parents to their preachers, to possibly even their school teachers (my daughter's high school biology teacher made an announcement at the start of the lesson on evolution that, as a Christian, she didn't believe in it, herself, but it was just part of the curriculum that they had to get through). They were taught all these misleading creationist arguments from people they trusted from a very young age. So the smartest kids were actually the best at absorbing those lessons. And since it takes a while for people to fully develop critical thinking skills, and a fair amount of discipline to go back and apply that to things you think you already know, it's hardly a surprise that those bright kids brought up within a creationist environment carried that belief into their adulthood. (And to be fair, ask yourself how you know that matter is composed of atoms and that atoms are composed of even smaller particles – do you really understand the evidence, or is it just common knowledge that you were taught back when you were younger?) I will say, though, that the number of intelligent, well-educated creationists I've met is rather small. You can definitely see a correlation vs. education level (note that graph is a bit old from 2005): SOURCE: Americans Weigh In on Evolution vs. Creationism in Schools So yes, I've met otherwise intelligent folks who were also creationists. But once you talk with them, it almost invariably turns out that, for whatever reason, they don't actually understand evolution. I have yet to meet a single person in real life who could accurately explain evolution yet still rejected it.
