If statistics are correct that one in ten men are gay, then which one of the twelve disciples of Christ was gay? One of them had to be a closet case. That’s not how probabilities work. Taking your statistic at face value, the probability that at least one of the 12 disciples was gay would be calculated as: 1 − ( 1 − p ) n 1 − ( 1 – 1 10 ) 12 71.8 % And sure, 71.8% is decently high odds, but it’s not guaranteed that “One of them had to be a closet case.” Take in other potential objections, such as whether or not that stat truly is accurate, or whether folks 2000 years ago even had the same conceptions of gay vs. straight as we do today, and it’s problematic to try to draw any conclusions around this.

Will drinking beer while still on a calorie deficit affect my fat loss? As the old saying goes – everything in moderation. If you don't drink in moderation, it can be a real whammy to weight loss. First you get all the calories from the beer itself. Beer can range anywhere from around 100 calories for an American light lager to over 300 calories for a Belgian triple. Drink a bunch of craft beers and IPAs for a night on the town with friends, and that could add up to a few thousand calories worth of beer alone. Then, you get the munchies that come along with that, combined with the lower inhibitions caused by the alcohol, and that 3 am trip to the drive thru (with your DD driving, of course) to pick up a double bacon cheeseburger with a large fries sounds like just the thing. Then you've got the hangover the next day, with yet more cravings for greasy fried foods, just adding to the calories. In short, aside from any of the other reasons to avoid overdoing it with beer, you definitely don't want to do so if you're trying to lose weight. But if you do stick to moderation, you should be fine. The key to losing weight is to consume less calories than you expend, and you don't need to stick to diet food to achieve that goal. I myself lost around 60 lbs by eating a normal balanced diet, just less of it. And yes, I still treated myself to occasional desserts and sweets, and usually a few beers over the weekend. Complete abstinence just leads to temptation.

Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? Yes, but a couple clarifications, first. First, it's not like any fish personally decided to grow limbs that were closer to legs than fins. Mutation really is a random process beyond the conscious control of the organisms experiencing those mutations. Just think about yourself. Did you choose any of the genetic mutations that differentiate you from your parents? If you have any children, did you choose any of the genetic mutations that got passed on to them? No, of course not. Such mutations are things that happen on a chemical level that we're never aware of. Heck, us people are just about the only organisms with the smarts to even understand genetics in the first place, so our ancient fish ancestors certainly weren't thinking about genetic mutations. Second, evolution of such big transitions is a gradual process that takes many, many generations to happen. It's not like there was a fish species that instantly evolved into a land dwelling animal, let alone into us humans. There were many stages along the way, from 'walking' underwater (similar to frogfish or certain walking sharks in the modern day), to slightly amphibious lifestyles (like some catfish), to even more amphibious lifestyles (like mudskippers), to something that's finally fully specialized for a life totally on land. Here's a diagram showing some of the stages along the fish to tetrapod transition, with some extra detail on the limbs, and how these limbs gradually went through this transition from fully aquatic to amphibious to fully terrestrial: ABOVE SOURCE: The origin of tetrapods Here's another figure to give a sense of the transition from those first tetrapods to us people. One thing that can sometimes be a bit misleading about diagrams like this is showing just a single path, perhaps giving the impression that this path was inevitably leading towards us. But you could make diagrams like this for any living creature, e.g. the path to mosquitos, the path to dandelions, or the path to a mushroom. And even in this path, at any critter on there, if you weren't specifically interested in human evolution, you could go off in a different direction to look at other creatures. For example, from Orrorin around 6 million years ago, you could go down a different path that led to chimpanzees rather than us people. Or from that Repenomamus around 230 million years ago, you could pick paths to any mammal alive today. ABOVE SOURCE: Visualized: The 4 Billion Year Path of Human Evolution And just to be clear, all of the animals shown in both of those figures are known from fossil remains, sometimes more than one specimen for each species. Just going with the first figure, here are some of the available fossils: ABOVE: Eusthenopteron SOURCE: File:Eusthenopteron foordi 1.jpg - Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia ABOVE: Panderichthys SOURCE: Panderichthys | Fossiilid.info ABOVE: Tiktaalik SOURCE: Famous fish fossil takes final bow in Philadelphia ABOVE: Acanthostega SOURCE: File:Acanthostega Deep Time.jpg - Wikimedia Commons ABOVE: Ichthyostega SOURCE: Ichthyostega Fossil Skeleton, First Fish to grow legs & move onto land ABOVE: Tulerpeton (I couldn't find an actual photo in a quick Google search, but this at least shows which bones were actually found – in white, and which are only inferred – in grey) SOURCE: Tulerpeton curtum by Ivanbel on DeviantArt

I totally believe the evolution theory because it has tons of scientific evidence, but I don't get it how marine life evolved to have lungs, limbs, developed, and somehow intelligent brain to live on land? I think part of the problem is people only think about a stereotypical, generic fish, and don't know about or don't think about the wide variety we see in living fish. You mentioned lungs and limbs, so let's take a look at those. And let's start with the limbs, since it makes for cooler videos. First, here's a frogfish. To be clear, frogfish aren't particularly closely related to the first tetrapods. They're adapted to a fully aquatic lifestyle without ever venturing onto land. But yet, they walk underwater, because it's a better way for them to get around, and especially to use their fins to sit on the ocean floor waiting to ambush prey. And here's a type of walking shark. Again, these are fully aquatic sharks. Their walking isn't some type of planning ahead for a life on the land, but a very useful means of locomotion to prowl around a reef. Next, let's move on to lungs. Air breathing is in fact quite common in many lineages of fish. Oxygen is much more consistent in the atmosphere than in the water, so many fish will surface to swallow gulps of air. Somewhere around 400 million years ago, the common ancestor of bony fish evolved a primitive lung as an outgrowth of the stomach as a way to improve oxygen absorption from these swallowed gulps. Over time, some lineages developed more advanced lungs, while others actually went in a different direction, and the lung evolved into a swim bladder. It just so happens that the lineage that evolved a swim bladder has gone on to become the most successful lineage of fish, so it somewhat biases our perception of what's normal. But a look at the bony fish family tree shows lungs to be rather widespread: ABOVE: The lineages in solid black still have lungs, while the lineages with the dashed outlines evolved swim bladders. SOURCE: How did fish evolve the ability to breathe on land? But even in the lineages that traded lungs for swim bladders, in certain environments, it's still beneficial for fish to be able to breathe air, and so various lineages have evolved new adaptations to allow this. Some fish, like bettas, are so dependent on atmospheric oxygen that they'll 'drown' if they can't get to the surface to take a breath. ABOVE SOURCE: Accessory Respiratory Organs of Fishes (With Diagram) | Chordata | Zoology So, just looking at living species of fish, walking and breathing air are relatively common. And from there, it's not a big step (get it?) to begin spending some time on land. Even that is common enough in living fish, from mudskippers to walking catfish to another species of walking shark that I didn't show here (Epaulette Shark Walks on Land). And once you have fish spending some time on land, well, it's not hard to see how they could become even more specialized to spend even more time on land. In other words, there's no need to ponder any special or unique conditions for why our ancestors would have evolved legs or lungs to make the transition from water to land, since we see plenty of analogs in fish alive right now. They’re simply useful features for some fish to have.

Why do most Americans prefer processed food and artificial over fresh and natural food? Because ‘processing’ isn’t the boogey man you think it is. Processed foods are delicious. And in many cases, the processing actually makes the foods safer and more nutritious. ABOVE SOURCE: The Truth About Eating Processed Foods — The Bodybuilding Dietitians Let me give an example. I like milk and dairy products. Only one time in my life have I I tried unprocessed milk, right after milking it from the cow. It was even still warm. But most of the time, I buy my milk from the grocery store, so I want it pasteurized to make sure it's safe from pathogens. I also like cheese and butter, which are both also processed foods (they're no longer simply raw milk). And for a lot of folks, the processing to make cheese or yogurt can reduce the lactose for people who have issues with that. Same thing with bread. I could eat bread all day. Raw, unprocessed wheat? Not so much. The grinding and cooking even make the nutrients easier to digest. And meat? Now, don't get me wrong. There's nothing wrong with a steak that's only minimally processed (butchering, seasoning, and cooking). But sausages, ham, and bacon? Oh man. A world without bacon would be a sad world indeed. And maybe you think I'm being a smartass, but I'm not. I'm going to guess that you weren't considering bread to be a processed food, but it is. Some foods may be processed more than others, but it's hard to draw any clear dividing line between what's too processed and what isn't. I mean, how does extra chopping or mixing magically make foods unhealthy? I've got the same pet peeves over 'artificial' ingredients. We don't have Star Trek replicators that can create molecules from scratch from energy. Everything we put into our food came from nature at some point. Where do you draw the line between natural and artificial ingredients? And even if you do have some threshold of chemistry that you'll use to designate 'artificial' ingredients, what does that have to do with health or safety? (As an example from medicine, we synthesize acetylsalicylic acid for aspirin, because it actually has less side effects than the naturally occurring salicylic acid found in willow bark that inspired the medicine.) And don't get me started on the silly saying that if you can't pronounce an ingredient, don't eat it. Have you ever seen all the chemical constituents of an egg? Practically all food is a complex mix of lots and lots of hard to pronounce chemicals. Most of those chemicals are safe. Some aren't. But whether or not they're safe has no correlation to how easy they are to pronounce. ABOVE SOURCE: Ingredients of an All-Natural Egg So yeah. I like sausage and bread and ham and pasteurized milk and all types of other processed foods I can buy from the grocery store. I eat processed food because I'm not a wild animal. While I was looking for images for processed foods, I came across many figures where people try to add an extra category, of ‘ultra processed’. Here’s one that was especially silly: ABOVE SOURCE: ABOVE SOURCE: MailOnline's guide to tell ultra-processed food apart They called French fries ultra processed. Sliced potatoes fried in oil. I’m not sure how much less processing you can do to a cooked food. And they’ve got ice cream on there. My family had a hand cranked ice cream maker when I was growing up, and we used it quite a bit for extended family get togethers. It’s just milk, cream, sugar, and a little vanilla, mixed up in a container surrounded by ice and rock salt. What’s ‘ultra processed’ about that? Now, I’m not saying an excess of fries and ice cream would make a healthy diet, but it’s got nothing to do with the amount of processing that went into making them.

Do people with little animal door flaps ever get unwelcome intruders in their homes? More than once. A Midnight Visitor The first time was close to my daughter's 15th birthday. And I know that specifically because we had a full house of relatives who were in town for her quinceañera. Our doggie/cat door was from the house to the garage. We then left the small back door of the garage open to the back yard, so that the cats and weenie dog could get in and out that way. We'd occasionally had issues with racoons in the past when I kept the dog food out in the garage, but after I started securing the lid better, they started leaving us alone. But that evening, we'd left the big garage door open, and a family of racoons got into the garage. We thought we'd chased them all out, so we completely shut all the outside garage doors, thinking that would keep the entire family out. Sometime around two in the morning, the weenie dog started barking and barking, waking up everybody in the house. I came downstairs, and there he was, with a baby racoon cornered in the family room and a gathering crowd of family members. I guess one of the racoon family had been left behind and found its way through the doggie door. My uncle told me it was just a baby so why don't I just go and grab it. I shot back why doesn't he go grab it. In the end, we called animal control, and they came and got it. A Nosy Neighbor We went for years without any more unexpected visitors to the house. In the meantime, our previous cats and dogs had all died, and we'd become roommates with a new cat, who started off feral using our garage, and who I was able to eventually coax into the house and teach him how to use the cat door. My wife named him Chester. He was a long haired tabby cat. There was another long haired tabby cat running around the neighborhood who looked very similar. At first, I named this other cat Not Chester. But I eventually learned that he was an actual pet who belonged to our neighbor two houses down, who we then began calling Sir William Wallace the Gentleman. Well, being a house cat himself, he understood the concept of cat doors, and I began catching him, or evidence of him, in the house on a pretty regular basis. It was especially irritating to find the butter I left out on the counter with a whole bunch of cat sized bites taken out. The last straw was when I was in our upstairs office working from home, and he had the audacity to come all the way upstairs to the room I was in. After that, I investigated higher tech options, and bought an electronic cat flap that you could program to only unlock for your specific cat's RFID chip (which meant Chester also got a trip to the vet to get chipped). Problem solved, mostly. A Thief in the Night One problem with this cat flap is that the way it locked under normal operation, it only blocked the flap from opening inward. For going out, the flap could still swing open. This worked fine for most animals, but racoons aren't most animals. We had a container full of pecans in the dining room, close to the garage door, and I came down one morning to find pecan shells all over the dining room floor. I didn't think too much about it, and just cleaned them up. But when it happened again, I knew there was a problem. It seems that the racoon had figured out how to get just enough of a grip on the flap to pull it open from the outside. Somewhat fortuitously, that was just around the time I was getting ready to head to El Paso for a month, taking Chester with me. So I set the cat flap to the completely locked mode (which wouldn't open in either direction), and put a trash can right in front of it on the inside of the house. I think the racoon figured out that his free meal ticket was over, so that seemed to put an end to it. Still a Nosy Neighbor Now that we've had the electronic flap for a couple years, it doesn't swing quite as freely as it did when new. So sometimes when Chester comes in, it won't swing back all the way shut to where it gets locked. And so, just a month or two ago, I was downstairs with Chester on my lap, when I heard something eating his cat food. I looked, and there was Sir William Wallace stealing Chester's food. So I chased him out again. So yeah, we've had our share of uninvited guests thanks to the doggie/cat door. The electronic one seems to have solved most of the problems, but it hasn't stopped them completely.

Evolutionists have been debating the chicken and chicken egg question for a long time. Can evolution explain which came first? No, because evolution helps us to understand that it's not the type of thing you can pinpoint. It would be like trying to define the precise second when dusk becomes night, or the precise date that a child becomes an adult. It just doesn't work that way. These are gradual processes that elude precise demarcations. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. In sexually reproducing animals, there's no single individual that's a different species from their parents, or indeed, the entire population of which they're a part. Plus, there's plenty of genetic variability within a population, which will be recombined in all types of different ways as the animals mate. Why did Tim Walz put female tampons and pads in the boys washroom? I have to say, this is one of the stranger tempests in a teapot I've seen in a while. The reality seems like such a mundane law (albeit very beneficial) that I’m surprised it’s managed to draw this much attention. But while most of the manufactured controversy came out of the right-wing, some left-wing responses have also been a bit more rationalization after the fact rather than what the law originally intended, and based more around conjecture than what's actually going on in Minnesota (i.e. it didn't have anything to do with logistics). So first – the civics lessons. Tim Walz didn't write this law. He didn't campaign on it or provide a draft for the legislature to act on. The law was originally sponsored by Sandra Feist in the Minnesota House, in a standalone bill, HF 44 , and then got included in the much larger Education Finance Bill, HF 2497. After going through the full process in the Minnesota House and Senate, the Education Finance Bill was eventually approved by majorities in both chambers, and so Tim Walz signed it into law. But this whole initiative of providing menstrual products to student was never something that Walz himself led. The main purpose of the law originally proposed by Feist is to provide menstrual products to students. This isn't some revolutionary idea new to Minnesota. There are similar laws on the books in 28 states and D.C. to address what some describe as "period poverty". According to Period Products in Schools, 1 in 4 students struggle to afford such products. And one study of a program in NYC found a 2.4% increase in attendance when free period products were offered to students. As one of the students who testified in the Minnesota House during a hearing on the legislation put it, "We cannot learn while we are leaking" (source: Minnesota may soon OK free menstrual products in schools. These teens led the way). ABOVE SOURCE: Period Products in Schools - Alliance for Period Supplies If you want to read the law for yourself, go to the full text of HF2497. It's easy to find the relevant portions. Just do a search for 'menstrual'. Here's the main portion: ARTICLE 1 GENERAL EDUCATION Section 1. [121A.212] ACCESS TO MENSTRUAL PRODUCTS. A school district or charter school must provide students with access to menstrual products at no charge. The products must be available to all menstruating students in restrooms regularly used by students in grades 4 to 12 according to a plan developed by the school district. For purposes of this section, "menstrual products" means pads, tampons, or other similar products used in connection with the menstrual cycle. There's another passage specifying that the budget for this will be "$2 times the adjusted pupil units of the school district for the school year", and another passage including these menstrual products in a list of allowed purposes for "Total operating capital revenue". Note that there's no mandate that tampons have to be supplied in the boys restroom. However, the language was gender neutral, allowing for discretion at the local levels for schools to implement this law. And that gender neutral language was on purpose. According to Feist, the sponsor of the original bill: While the vast majority of the period products will be used in the girls’ bathrooms, the decision was made to structure the bill as gender-inclusive in order to ensure that trans and nonbinary students who menstruate would have equal access to the products they need. SOURCE: Yes, Tim Walz signed a law requiring Minnesota public schools to provide free tampons in school bathrooms Also, as noted in the article, Why Republicans are calling Walz 'Tampon Tim' — and why Democrats embrace it, there was opposition to this gender inclusivity when "Some Minnesota Republicans initially tried to limit the initiative to female-assigned and gender-neutral bathrooms, but were unsuccessful." However, it's interesting to note that the Republican who proposed that amendment did go on to support the final bill, as he felt the overall issue was important, and not worth killing over that compromise. It’s also worth pointing out that schools are free to come up with their own plans to implement the law. According to an editorial from the Minnesota based Star Tribune, A reality check on the ‘Tampon Tim’ meme: At Anoka-Hennepin, the state’s largest school district, the free products are not found in traditional male-only bathrooms, a spokesman said. But they are provided for free to all in “nongendered bathrooms,” girls’ bathrooms or from health staffers. I can't say that absolutely no schools in Minnesota have provided tampons in the boys room, but if the largest school district in the state isn't doing so, it's obviously not a requirement of the law, so long as transgender students can still receive menstrual products if they need them. So basically, Tim Walz signed a large law that had a bunch of different sections dealing with multiple aspects of education funding. Among these was a requirement to provide tampons to students for free, which seems utterly reasonable to me. The language was made specifically gender neutral, allowing individual schools to implement the law as they saw fit, so long as they were still complying and supporting all students who needed menstrual products, which also seems pretty reasonable to me. And just to be clear, the law doesn't actually force schools to provide tampons in the boys room, and as proven in practice, at least one school district cited in the news hasn't.

What accidents or incidents have you personally had with deep fryers? Back when I was in high school, I got a job at KFC. There was a certain minimum level for the shortening in the pressure fryers, but they never actually gave us any formal training on proper technique to add more. The method I developed for myself was to cut off a chunk of shortening (it was solid at room temperature), then stab that chunk with the knife, and lower it down into the fryer. That seemed better to me than just throwing the chunk in there and having the hot grease splash. Well, one day, I had a just gotten a big chunk of shortening over the fryer when it fell off of the knife, and sent a huge splash of grease up at my head. I managed to turn to the side and close my eyes, but the grease got half of my face. I immediately went to the sink in the kitchen, and began running cold water over my face. The manager didn't seem to quite know what to do, and couldn't get a hold of my parents, so eventually, somebody gave me a ride home. When I did get home, my parents were out in the yard working (why they never heard the phone – this was a bit before cell phones), and were quite surprised to see me, especially with half my face burnt. So they immediately threw me into the car and drove me to the ER. The ER took me in right away (no waiting around like when you've merely got the sniffles), took me straight to a room, and then promptly treated me with nothing fancier than cold washcloths. Really, that was the only treatment – a basin of ice water with a few washcloths soaking in it, that my mom would swap out when the one on my face started to warm up too much. After a couple hours to draw out as much heat as possible, they sent me on my way with referrals for follow ups. Over the next few days, my face started to look bad. Luckily, it was mostly 'just' second degree burns. But once those blisters started popping and oozing puss all over my face, I was not a pretty sight. One of those referrals was a plastic surgeon, but the only real treatment I needed was bacitracin to prevent infection. All this happened just a couple weeks before graduation. Any open wounds had mostly healed in time, but the skin was still pretty tender, and I was supposed to keep out of the sun. So, I went everywhere with a wide brimmed hat, and avoided sitting out under the sun for all of the graduation rehearsals. I also avoided shaving, so I had that just wrong 17 year old level of stubble – more scruffy than rugged. A couple friends and I had also planned a cross country road trip right after graduation, which meant upgrading our provisional drivers licenses to full licenses, so we wouldn't have any restrictions driving during the trip. Oh man was that a horrible drivers license photo, between the scruff, red face, and completely unkempt hair once I took off the wide brimmed hat. Whenever anybody complained about a bad drivers license photo, I always had them beat (and they always agreed). Thankfully, I only developed a few minor scars, that weren't even that obvious when I was clean shaven, but are now completely hidden by my (adult) beard. Anyway, I was more careful adding shortening after that. I even got workman’s comp out of it.

Do pro-choice people at least think we should reduce the number of abortions? That's a weird question. It's about like asking if we should reduce the number of bypass surgeries for clogged arteries. On the one hand, as the old saying goes, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. It would be great if we could get people to live healthier lifestyles to avoid clogged arteries and the need for bypass surgeries in the first place. But as long as people do have clogged arteries, I very much want bypass surgery to be available. I don't want to reduce the number of bypass surgeries if the need still remains. And it still remains a fact of life that clogged arteries will happen regardless, so some amount of bypass surgeries will always be necessary. It's similar for abortion. It would be great if everybody had comprehensive sex education and easily available contraception and birth control to reduce the number of accidental pregnancies. And it would be great to have generally good living conditions for all families, easily affordable and accesible prenatal care, or at least adequate social safety nets, so that nobody was worried about having the means to raise a child with a good quality of life and opportunities. And it would be really great if there were no more rapes, developmental abnormalities, or other complications with pregnancies. So of course it would be nice to reduce all the reasons for abortions in the first place. But I don't want to reduce access to abortions while the need remains. And it's still a fact of life that some amount of abortions will always be necessary, because we never will fully eliminate all those reasons. So yes, like with any other healthcare issue, it would be best to reduce the causes that lead to needing medical intervention. But as long as the need's still there, you still provide the healthcare. And it's just a weird way to phrase a question, asking if we want to reduce a specific medical procedure, rather than addressing the causes that lead to that procedure.

What is the evolutionary reason for biological ageing? It's often helpful to think of evolution in terms of reproduction. As my one friends put it, "Forget survival of the fittest – the only reason survival is important in evolution is because you cannot reproduce when you're dead."* And while all things being equal, staying alive forever would certainly enable you to make more babies, all things aren't equal. Even if we didn't die of old age, something would end up killing us eventually – accidents, infections, predators, etc. Depending on the specific organism and its niche, there's some age by which it's overwhelmingly likely to be dead, anyway. On top of that, consider that maintaining a body doesn't come for free. It takes calories to repair injuries, maintain an immune system, suppress cancer, etc. And calories that are going towards that maintenance aren't going towards reproduction (mating, raising babies, defending territories, etc.). So, evolution finds a balance – put enough calories into maintenance to live long enough to reproduce, but just enough to maintain your body until the odds are likely that you'd be dead from something else, anyway. Since there's so little chance of any organisms within a certain species surviving past that age, it doesn't matter what happens to their bodies after that. You can see how this plays out by comparing the lifespans of different species. Something like a whale, which has very few natural predators, does have a very high likelihood of surviving year to year, so they have evolved to put significant energy into maintaining their bodies – over a century, in some cases. Same thing for large land tortoises on the Galapagos Islands. They do benefit by surviving for many breeding seasons, since it gives them that many more opportunities to reproduce. But something like a mouse, which is being hunted by everything from rattlesnakes to housecats to owls, isn't likely to last long in this world. Their best bet is to have as many offspring as quickly as they can, before something kills them, and not waste much energy on maintaining their bodies. Consequently, even if raised in captivity, mice won't live much past 1 to 3 years. Unlike some popular misconceptions might imply, it has nothing to do with gene turnover to promote evolution, or older generations making way for the next generation to avoid competing over resources (because honestly, from an evolutionary perspective, outside your own personal offspring, who gives a damn about the neighbor's kids – they're not carrying your genes**). It's because death is inevitable, so evolution finds the right balance of maintaining your body for long enough, and then putting everything else it can into reproduction. * That quote is from Scott Solomon, in his book, Future Humans: Inside the Science of Our Continuing Evolution: Solomon, Scott: 9780300208719: Amazon.com: Books ** Of course, that's oversimplifying things a bit. Kin selection does mean that it's beneficial to help relatives besides just your direct offspring. And various strategies of cooperation can be mutually beneficial even among non-related organisms. Still, it's never in an organism's evolutionary interests to sacrifice its own reproductive success for the sake of a non-relative.

Do atheists think that theists are unintelligent? It's complicated. So, let's get the provocative part out of the way, first. Numerous studies have found a negative correlation between intelligence and being religious. In other words, the less intelligent a person is, the more likely they are to be religious. And the more intelligent a person is, the more likely they are to be an atheist or agnostic. For example, one study that surveyed 432 people (The Relationship Between Religiousness/Spirituality and Psychometric Intelligence in the United States) found Christians to have an average IQ of 96.7, compared to 104.9 for atheists and 107.5 for agnostics. There was also a meta analysis (The Negative Intelligence–Religiosity Relation: New and Confirming Evidence) that synthesized the results of 83 prior studies, finding a negative correlation that ranged from -0.20 to -0.23. But, it's important to keep in mind that these are only averages, and that a correlation of -0.2 isn't very strong. Here are some examples of correlations, to give you an idea of what -0.2 looks like: SOURCE: https://quizlet.com/514729056/statistics-flash-cards/ As you might expect from the above, there's also quite a bit of overlap between religious and non-religious folks. If you were to plot bell curves of the IQs of those two groups, it would look something like this: SOURCE: Unwarranted Assumption There is lots of overlap, with plenty of religious folks among the most intelligent people, and plenty of non-religious folks that aren't the sharpest knives in the drawer. It's trivial to find examples of intelligent Christians (e.g. List of Christians in science and technology - Wikipedia). I follow plenty of intelligent Christians, myself, here on Quora. Is it general intelligence that makes the difference, specific types of intelligence, or even learned skillsets that allow some people to do better on these types of tests? But overall, there have been enough studies with similar results, that it's safe to say that non-believers are on average slightly more intelligent than believers. Still, the correlation is so small that it doesn't tell you much about individual believers or non-believers.

Why can't English rugby be as popular as American football in the USA? Well, they started off from the same roots, but then developed along independent paths in their respective countries. So it's no wonder that the version that developed in the USA is more popular in the USA. Both rugby and gridiron football, along with the various other types of football, grew out of a family of British games known as mob football, with different 'house rules' among every group in every town and village that played it. Since it was British colonists who were the first Europeans to come to what would become the U.S. and Canada, they brought along their British sports, including mob football. Round about the mid 1800s, social conditions were finally ripe to begin formalizing these diverse rules with different governing bodies. At the time, the Rugby School's rules were very similar to the rules at several American and Canadian colleges like Harvard, McGill, and Yale (in contrast to the association football rules of Cambridge and the Sheffield Football Club). The New World teams went on to develop new innovations that moved the sport further away from its cousin, rugby, including the line of scrimmage, a system of downs, and then in 1906 the forward pass (Walter Camp was especially influential in many of these innovations). ABOVE: An 1895 football game between Auburn and Georgia looking a lot more like rugby than modern day gridiron football SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia ABOVE: Another pre-forward pass college football game – the University of Minnesota vs. the University of Michigan in 1902 SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia So basically, the two sports started off largely the same, but then went down separate paths in each country. So of course the rules that developed in the USA are more popular here. If most Americans had wanted to play a game more similar to rugby, they wouldn't have changed the rules in the first place.

On what basis did evolutionists decide humans have a close common ancestry with apes, was it by looks? If so what about the kangaroo and the sloth? If by DNA, what about the banana? If it was by intelligence, what about the octopus? Carl Linnaeus is known as the father of modern taxonomy. He developed the now traditional system that you probably learned in high school biology – Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. This system is a nested hierarchy that we now recognize as being due to evolutionary relatedness, but Linaeus himself was a creationist (he died before Darwin was even born), and was merely trying to recognize the pattern of God's creation. And he based his system largely on physical similarity. Of course, he went deeper than superficial resemblances, and looked at the entire anatomy of organisms. That is how, for example, he recognized that dolphins and whales were mammals and not fish. And Linnaeus recognized the obvious anatomical similarities between humans and other apes, putting humans, chimpanzees, and orangutans all in the same genus, Homo (gorillas weren't yet known to European naturalists, or he almost surely would have included them, as well). I mean, the similarities between humans and other apes is sometimes so striking it's almost eerie: ABOVE SOURCE: Bonobo photos by Frans de Waal Kangaroos and sloths aren't nearly so anatomically similar to humans as the other apes. I mean, yes they're both mammals, so they're more related to humans than, say, a magpie or an oak tree, but not at that same level of similarity as the other apes. I mean, kangaroos are marsupials, for heaven's sake, with many, may differences to us placental mammals. Linnaeus recognized this over 200 years ago. DNA wasn't recognized as our hereditary molecule until the 1940s, and it's only been in more recent decades that scientists have been able to sequence DNA and otherwise study it in much more detail. Much like the anatomical comparisons that Linnaeus pioneered, you can also compare the similarity of the DNA of different organisms, and construct nested hierarchies of similarity. And when scientists did this, the resulting 'trees' matched up nearly spot on with the trees developed from traditional classification. In other words, while we knew from anatomical comparisons that humans were more closely related to apes than to sloths, DNA studies found exactly the same thing. So you have two different lines of evidence to do these comparisons, yet they produce essentially the same results. You mentioned bananas. Bananas are only distantly related to us people, and the genetics confirms this. While our DNA is roughly 98% the same with chimpanzees (it depends on how exactly you're doing the comparison), it's only around 50% the same with bananas. But bananas are multicellular eukaryotes, so even they are more closely related to us than some other life forms. Bacteria, for example, are even more distant relatives, with even less DNA in common with us. Your last question is about intelligence. The thing about lots of evolutionary traits is that they can develop separately through convergent evolution. When this happens, although the traits might have superficial resemblance, there will be lots of differences in the details. And octopuses and other cephalopods have brains that are very different from us mammals. They developed their intelligence through a completely different evolutionary path than us. So yes, anatomical similarities and genetic similarities are both used to determine the relatedness of organisms. But intelligence is a trait that can evolve independently, so it’s not as useful on its own.

Can airplanes sometimes not store fuel in their tanks due to weight limitations? If this is the case, what are the alternatives for storing fuel in an airplane or other vehicle? Airplanes are much more weight sensitive than the cars that most people are used to. Cars have fuel tanks that will typically let you drive somewhere around 5 hours before needing to refuel. And you don't need to worry all that much about how much you load up your car. It can be just you driving by yourself, or loading up the whole family with luggage. Your gas mileage might go down a bit, but unless you're looking at really heavy cargo, you don't have to worry about overloading the car. Planes, on the other, don't have that luxury. You get a combined 'useful load', which is how much you can load up an airplane before it becomes too heavy to fly. It's up to the operator to decide how much of that useful load to devote to passengers and other payload, and how much to devote to fuel. Take the Cessna 172 as an example, one of the most iconic general aviation airplanes. It has 4 seats, a useful load of 878 lbs, and gas tanks that can hold 318 lbs of fuel. If you're running the math in your head, you can see that if you filled up the tanks with fuel, you'd only have 560 lbs of payload left, which may be fine if you're flying by yourself, but doesn't leave a lot of weight for 4 passengers and luggage, especially if they're adults. ABOVE: A screenshot from Cessna’s website, with appropriate text for a discussion about fuel burn SOURCE: Cessna Skyhawk Piston | Textron Aviation But, that 318 lbs of fuel is enough to let you fly for over 5 hours. Do you really need to fly that long if you're just taking some friends up for a sight-seeing flight around town, or for the clichéd $100 hamburger at the next airport over? Probably not. So, you might only load up half the fuel, which still lets you fly over 2 ½ hours, but leaves you 719 lbs for passengers and other payload, which is getting much more reasonable for 4 people (not necessarily 4 large adults, but at least a mix of larger and more petit folks). It's all about giving the operator options. You could make the full fuel payload seem higher by giving them a smaller gas tank, but then they wouldn't have the freedom to fly longer flights. Or you could just give it two seats, but then they wouldn't have the freedom to carry more passengers. So, you give them the ability to decide how they want to use the plane. For the big boys in airliners, it's a lot of the same considerations. Is it a short haul flight between close cities? Only load as much fuel as you need and then cram it full of passengers. Is it a long range flight? Well, you might have to go lighter on the cargo. So to answer the question directly, yes, sometimes airplanes don't fill up the wing tanks in order to be able to carry more payload. But other times it's the opposite, filling up the tanks and carrying less payload. It's all up to the specific mission.

Young Earth creationists like to use Bishop Ussher's calculated date for when the Earth was created. Who else has done the calculations to confirm it? I've gone through a portion of the estimate, myself*. You can read a good summary of Ussher's estimate on Wikipedia. Basically, he broke it down into three portions (note that the timespans are the ones that Ussher calculated, not mine): Ussher then used other sources outside the Bible to determine the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Since the first two portions of the estimate are so straightforward, they were easy enough to double check. Creation to Exodus Like I said, this part is easy enough to look up yourself in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. The only real minor cases of uncertainty in there are when Noah had Shem, and when Nahor had Terah, since the wording used is a tad ambiguous. In the first case, per Genesis 5:32: After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. In the latter case, per Genesis 11:26: When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Those sons weren't triplets, so you have to decide whether those ages are when those guys started having kids, or when they'd finally had all three. Folks who care more about this than I do (like Ussher) have tried to get to the bottom of it. I just used those numbers as is, since it's still in the ballpark. Anyway, here's my table of going from Adam to the birth of Abraham: So, it comes out to 1949 years. Next, take a look at Genesis 12:4: So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. So, Abraham was 75 years old at the start of the events in Exodus. Add those two numbers together, and you get 2024 years from the creation of Adam to the start of the events in Exodus. Ussher came up with 2082. Maybe that's to do with the aforementioned issues around Noah and Terah, or the time between the start of the events of in Exodus and actually escaping, or maybe even which source of the Bible he was using (they don't all have the same ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11), but those numbers are certainly in the same ballpark. Exodus to Solomon's Temple The next part is really easy. Per 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. So, you've got 480 years from the Exodus until the building of Solomon's Temple. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity After that, it takes more effort than I was willing to put into it to trace the reigns of all the kings of Israel and Judah. But just to give a taste, here's 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. So go searching for all those types of verses, and you can work out how long it was until the crowning of king Amel-Marduk. Ussher apparently made some judgment calls on overlapping periods, working out his estimate of 424 years. Somewhat independently, but not nearly as precisely, there are unbroken genealogies in the Gospels from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, they do contradict each other, but we'll just look past that. Matthew lists 42 generations from Adam to Jesus, while Luke lists 77. In either case, those give ballpark estimates on the order of thousands of years, even with the unrealistically high generation times in the early books of the Bible. So, the first two portions of that estimate are really pretty straight forward. And they rely on what seem to be matter of fact, boring ancestral lists, not fables, parables, or allegorical moral tales. Sure, it might seem unbelievalbe for a guy to be having kids at 500 years old, but is it really more unbelievable than the Plagues of Egypt or other Bible stories? And the third part, while I didn't go through the numbers, is from the part of the Bible that's actually probably more historically reliable. Even with just the portions I did for myself, if you take those ancestry lists at more or less face value, they get you all the way to Solomon's Temple, going through Egyptian Pharaohs along the way. In the grand scheme of things, that's not that long ago. Assuming for the sake of argument that Solomon and the First Temple really existed, you're looking at a Bronze Age civlization, so somewhere on the order of 1000 BC. So going back 2500 years from that gets you to 3500 BC. So once again, we're in the same ballpark as Ussher. My takeaway after going through all this, is that Ussher was a lot more reasonable than certain quarters of the Internet give him credit for. Sure, you have to accept the Bible as more or less true in the first place. But once you do, his estimate just follows from simple statements of 'fact' within the Bible. Even the slight uncertainties and judgment calls are only on the order of decades (at least for a particular Bible with given numbers) and aren't going to push the dates around all that much. Basically, if you accept Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 as factual, you’ll end up with an estimate somewhere on par with Ussher’s. If you want to reconcile the Bible with the true age of the Earth, you have to explain why Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 aren’t meant to be taken at their word.** *Parts of this answer were adapted and/or copied from a previous answer along similar lines: **And yes. Plenty of Christians do say that Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 aren’t meant to be taken at their word. I’m just pointing out that Ussher was merely following the text.

If someone was hypothetically able to view the light that left Earth 65 million years ago during the Cretaceous period, what would they see and witness? I assume you picked 65 million years hoping to see dinosaurs. But in reality, you’re going to see something like this: ABOVE SOURCE: Jwst Feed (@jwstfeed.bsky.social) Yes, that’s an entire galaxy, not a single solar system, let alone a single planet like Earth. That is the galaxy known as NGC 3972, which is around 60–65 million light years away. This image was captured with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which is one of the most powerful telescopes ever built. Here’s another photo of the same galaxy by another incredibly powerful telescope, Hubble: ABOVE SOURCE: NGC 3972 - Wikipedia The issue is that 65 million light years is a long way away. The other issue is that telescopes can only ‘magnify’ an image so much. Because of the wave nature of light, as opposed to being pure rays, there’s essentially a limit to how much you can focus the image depending on how big your mirror is. That in turn limits how much detail you can make out. It’s not an issue of cramming a higher resolution scanner into your telescope. That would just give you a higher resolution of an out of focus image. I’ve gone through the math before in other answers. But if you wanted to make out a triceratops to roughly the resolution shown below from 65 million light years away, you would need a telescope 260 light years in diameter. That’s not gonna happen. Even solar gravitational lens telescope proposals only increase the effective diameter to that of a star, which is still well short of 260 light years. (That’s Galileo in the bottom right for scale, by the way.) The other issue that people tend not to think about is exposure times. If you look up the image info for NGC 3972 at HubbleSite.org, it lists exposure dates from April - July, 2015. Now, I’m not sure if it was focused on that single galaxy for the entire time. But still, you’re looking at a long exposure time to generate such an image. So if you were hoping to see individual dinosaurs, they’re not going to sit still that long for a portrait. Basically, with any type of realistic telescope technology, the best your going to do is a nice picture of the Milky Way galaxy. Maybe you’ll be able to pick out the Sun, but trying to image Earth on it’s own, let alone in any detail to see individual animals, just ain’t gonna happen. Related answers:

Has an airplane ever gone around the Earth west or east all the way? Yes, many people have done this. So let's take a look at a few of the more memorable ones. Douglas World Cruisers The very first successful attempt to fly around the world in an airplane was all the way back in 1924, not all that long after airplanes were first invented. It was a team of aviators with the U.S. Army Air Service. They flew special built airplanes named Douglas World Cruisers. They were in a bit of an unofficial race against competing teams from Italy, Portugal, and England (French and British teams had already made failed attempts in 1922 and 1923). ABOVE: A Douglas World Cruise in Flight SOURCE: Douglas World Cruiser - Wikipedia The team started off the journey with 8 aviators in 4 planes, leaving from Santa Monica, California, traveling east to west. One plane crashed relatively early in the attempt in Alaska (though thankfully the crew survived). A second plane had to ditch enroute from the Orkney Islands to Iceland after an oil pump failure, and then capsized and sank during the recovery effort (after the crew had already been safely taken aboard the ship attempting the recovery). But 4 of the aviators and 2 of the planes completed the journey, returning to Santa Monica 175 days after they'd begun. ABOVE: The path of the first successful circumnavigation by plane SOURCE: First aerial circumnavigation - Wikipedia Graf Zeppelin Cheating a bit on the question’s exact topic of ‘airplanes’, the famous dirigible, the Graf Zeppelin, became the first airship to fly around the world in 1929. With major funding from the American business magnate, William Randolph Hearst, the flight began from Lakehurst, New Jersey, flying west to east. At the start of the journey, the ship had a crew of 40 with 22 passengers, though it seems that some crew were left behind on some legs to help lighten the load. One of the passengers, Lady Grace Drummond-Hay, became the first woman to fly across the Pacific Ocean. The entire trip took just over 21 days. ABOVE SOURCE: Graf Zeppelin visits Tokyo, 1929. | Old Tokyo More Info: Round the World Flights Wiley Post The first person to fly solo around the world was Wiley Post, in his famous (and beautiful) airplane, the Winnie Mae (a Lockheed Vega), in 1933. He'd already flown a circumnavigation two years earlier with another aviator on board, Harold Gatty, as his navigator. His solo flight started and ended in Floyd Bennett Field in New York, and took a little under 8 days, flying west to east. Sadly, he died just a few years later attempting to cross the North Pole, with humorist Will Rogers aboard. ABOVE: A Painting of the Winnie May In Flight (which I can't seem to find the proper credit for). Just look at those sleek lines. SOURCE: https://www.flickr.com/photos/57440551@N03/38987333934 Voyager The first airplane to make the journey non-stop and without refueling was purpose designed and built by Burt Rutan, the Voyager, in 1986. The aircraft had two engines (one in the nose, one in the tail) to generate enough power to take off and climb with the weight of all that fuel, and then shut down the front engine once in cruise to reduce fuel consumption. Taking off from Edwards Air Force Base in California, the weight of all the fuel in the wings actually caused the wing tips to scrape during the takeoff roll, damaging the wing tips, but aerial inspection by a chase plane determined the aircraft to be good enough to continue the attempt. Flying east to west, they completed the flight in 9 days. ABOVE SOURCE: From Point A to Point A Breitling Orbiter The first balloon to fly non-stop around the world was the Breitling Orbiter 3. ABOVE SOURCE: Bertrand Piccard - Exploration - Breitling Orbiter Piloted by Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones, the balloon began its journey in Switzerland, caught a southwest wind to take it to the 9° west longitude line, and then caught east blowing winds to carry it around the world, eventually touching down in Egypt. ABOVE SOURCE: Weather and Climate: Let's talk about the weather Freedom Flight Perhaps this isn't the most famous circumnavigation flight, but it's an interesting one in the choice of aircraft. Back in 2003, two pilots, Ricky De Agrela and Alan Honeybourne set off in a pair of ultralights on an around the world expedition. Starting in their home country of South Africa, it was a 64000 km trek to go around the world and back to their starting point, though if I remember correctly, with ferrying across the Pacific. Tragically, Honeybourne was killed during the trip in a crash in China, and then his replacement, Martin Walker, was also killed in a crash in Belize. Still, De Agrela persevered, and completed the trip 11 months later in 2004. ABOVE SOURCE: Freedom Flight Of course, there were many more round the world flights besides those, such as the first to go around the poles in a Boeing 707 in 1965 (rather than east-west or west-east), Concorde setting the speed records for both east to west and west to east in 1992 and 1995, respectively, the first solo non-stop, non-refueled flight by Steve Fossett in 2005, or the first solar powered circumnavigation in the Solar Impulse in 2009. Actually, just a couple years ago in 2022, Mack Rutherford set a new record as the youngest pilot to fly solo around the world at just 17 years old. If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? The short answer is not much. The long answer is complicated, depending on exactly what you mean by bicycles and how much freedom you'll allow in interpreting the question. The first thing to note, that many people don't seem to realize, is that pedaling to power a generator gets harder and harder the more electrical power you have to provide. They just see the wires, and seem to think that it's no harder than pedaling a free-wheeling bike. But once you try to actually create current with those wires, they create magnetic fields. And those magnetic fields make it more difficult to turn the generator. The more power, the stronger the magnetic field, and the harder it is to pedal. It all goes back to the conservation of energy, and the fact that you can't get something for nothing. Moving on, if you mean stationary cycles, where instead of moving, you're just driving a generator, then you're not going to get much energy at all. Loring Chien already went through the math in his answer. Even taking it to the extreme of people riding such machines for 12 hours a day every day, you only get 10% of the world's electric consumption (the average person can only maintain around 50 - 100 W continuously). And of course, that extreme scenario is not at all practical. You can't do your real job when riding a stationary bike. So if you cut people’s time down to a somewhat more realistic 1 hr per day to leave them time to do other things, then you’re looking at less than 1% of the world’s electric consumption. But even that’s over-estimating the net results. If people are going to perform that much physical exercise daily, their calorie requirements are going to go up. That means more food needs to be grown, stored, and transported, and all of that takes energy. How much of that energy comes from electricity vs. petroleum based fuel is dependent on how quickly EVs displace IC engines, but it’s certainly going to be something (and non-negligible when you’re talking about changes to diet on the scale of the entire world’s population). If you meant adding a generator to regular bikes that generated electricity during the course of normal riding, the numbers come out even lower. Recalling that you can’t get something for nothing, a generator that’s driven through a direct mechanical connection is going to feel like riding the brakes, with the braking force being higher the more power you try to generate. Alternatively, a wind powered generator is going to increase your drag, again forcing you to have to pedal harder. Basically, since you need power to propel the bike, you have to settle for only a fraction of the power that the person can generate going to the generator. That’s why existing generators on bikes are only used for very lower power applications like lights. In short, you’ll generate well, well short of even the 1% from the previous scenario. What about the power savings if everybody rode bikes instead of driving in cars? Now, you’re looking at a double impact, because bikes are much smaller than cars and so don’t require as much power. i.e. The benefit is not just in using human power, but in not needing as much power to begin with. Of course, if you’re just looking at electricity, this is going to be a bigger effect as EVs become more common. What makes this complicated to analyze is that cycling can only replace some uses of automobiles, not all of them, so you have to take that into account. Here’s one study, Ditching the car for walking or biking just one day a week cuts carbon footprint,. If we take CO2 as a proxy for energy consumption, that study found “If just 10% of the population were to change travel behaviour, the emissions savings would be around 4% of lifecycle CO2 emissions from all car travel.” Based on a couple other sources (the Energy Information Administration and the Bureau of Tranpsportation Statistics), transportation in total makes up 37% of U.S. energy consumption, while light-duty short wheelbase vehicles (i.e. cars) makes up 40.3% of that, or around 15% of the total energy consumption. So a 4% savings on automobiles is around a half percent total energy savings. But if you upped that “10% of the population” to “100% of the population”, and it scaled linearly to a 40% savings on car travel, you’d end up with a 6% savings in total energy consumption. That’s not exactly huge, but it’s not negligible, either. To sum up, none of the scenarios result in huge energy savings. Loring Chien’s calculation of people riding all day, every day, still only results in 10% of the world’s electricity requirements. Reducing people’s time on the bikes to 1 hr a day drops that to less than 1%. Putting generators on existing bikes for transportation generates an even smaller percentage than that. The most realistic and achievable scenario is to get people to ride their bikes instead of driving their cars for trips where it’s feasible. Depending on how many people you can get to do this, you’re looking at around 0.5% total energy savings in a more feasible scenario, or 6% in an overly optimistic scenario. But a few percent here and a few percent there can eventually add up to significant savings.

What is the reasoning behind atheists thinking it's illogical to believe in god? Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs without being challenged by others? Let's take your latter two questions first: Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs... Yes without being challenged by others? Absolutely not. This is the type of delicate little snowflake mentality that so many people complain about. All beliefs should be robust enough that they can withstand inspection. If they're not, then maybe they weren't such good beliefs in the first place. Now, I'm not saying life needs to be one continuous debate during all waking hours. There's a time and place for everything, and there's a difference between debate and badgering (or to make a verb of a different animal, sea lioning). But yes, you should at least occasionally have discussions with people who disagree with you about challenging topics – politics, religion, morality, pineapple on pizza, etc. If you never challenge yourself, you'll never grow. And if you limit yourself to echo chambers of only like minded people, you'll never truly understand the wider world and why different people do things differently from you. I can think of plenty of examples from my own life where I'm grateful to the people who challenged me and helped me to see things differently. As far as your first question, well, that could be an entire book. But the short of it is, all the evidence we do have for God and Christianity is best explained as a mythology that developed out of previous mythologies. Heck, we even have evidence of Yahweh's origins in the Canaanite pantheon as a storm god – NOT the one and only God and creator of the universe. Other religions and their holy books are largely similar in that they've developed over generations as mythology. And the other big, glaring problem that they all have is a complete lack of credible evidence. Oh sure, Hindus, Buddhists, Christians, and Muslims all get warm fuzzy feelings when they pray, and some even manage to convince themselves that unlikely events and coincidences are evidence of their particular god(s) (but obviously, not the other gods). But this evidence hardly ever seems credible to outsiders who don't already share their beliefs. So there you go. We think it's not reasonable to believe in gods in general because there's no good evidence, and the capital G God in particular because the evidence we do have shows that he's a product of human myth making. And while we all certainly have a right to hold any beliefs we want, we should also be open to being challenged about those beliefs. That's the only way we grow as individuals.

If Christianity is wrong, then why do people believe in it? Before getting into the why, let's get a little perspective. Here is the breakdown of global religious affiliation: SOURCE: The Changing Global Religious Landscape That's a lot of diversity of religions, and none of them are believed by a majority of the world's population. And since many of these religions are mutually contradictory, it stands to reason that most of them are wrong. So, your question isn't just applicable to Christianity. It's applicable to all religions. Why do people believe them, when logically, most of them must be wrong? A big reason is the cognitive bias that Deborah Kelemen has coined 'promiscuous teleology', which is a tendency to see purpose and intention even when it's not really there. Here's an explanation from one paper on the topic, Teleology and the intentions of supernatural agents: Given that according to PT [promiscuous teleology], teleological reasoning develops from an early understanding of intentionality which is then overextended (Kelemen, 1999a), the notion of agency is central to teleology. This is because the only things capable of having intentions are things with minds, and the only things with minds are agents. In this view, just as “chairs are for sitting on” is true only if an agent intends the chair to serve this function, the statement “clouds rain so that plants can grow” is based in the misbelief that plants growing is the intended function of the cloud raining. The difference between these two teleological explanations is that whereas the former implies the intentions of a natural agent (a human), the latter seems to imply the intentions of a supernatural agent. And here's the abstract from a different paper, Promiscuous Teleology: From Childhood Through Adulthood and from West to East: From infancy we continually try to make sense of what goes on around us. One strategy in making sense of things is to look for how things might be purposeful or designed. So useful is this strategy that sometimes it gets overused—what Deborah Keleman calls promiscuous teleology . This chapter reviews research with children and adults across cultures—including recent work in China —that demonstrates that promiscuous teleology is a conceptual default that all peoples share but that may be tamped down through enculturation. Kelemen argues that this teleological reasoning makes certain religious ideas about supernatural agents’ activity in creating or ordering the world largely intuitive. Or to summarize all that, our tendency to see agency everywhere makes us prone to supernatural explanations. Now, there are further questions as to why we might have evolved this cognitive bias in the first place. As I noted in another answer, "There are various explanations for why we might have evolved this bias – from being social animals and having to understand intentions of our fellow humans, to being prodigious tool makers and having an instinctual sense of 'function' for items. And there's no reason the explanations need to be mutually exclusive. (And even all that is assuming it's an adaptive trait, and not just a spandrel of San Marco.)" Add in how children credulously accept lessons from their parents (and understandably so – there's too much knowledge to pass down any other way), and culture, and how these stories morph and change over the generations, and you've got the perfect recipe for a large diversity of supernatural stories to explain various aspects of our world. Christianity just happens to be one of these myths among many.

Will America ever eventually switch to the metric system of measurement for all applications? Eh. Maybe eventually. It seems like we're already slowly transitioning that way. There are certain measurements where metric has been used in the U.S. pretty much my whole life – the sciences (especially at universities), electrical power, measuring volumes of beverages (750 ml, 2 liter bottles, etc.). And there are some where I've seen the switch in my lifetime – particularly U.S. automakers – I only need my 'standard' sockets for classic cars, these days. But there are plenty of areas of society that haven't made the switch, and some of those seem like there's a lot of momentum resisting any change. My own field of aerospace engineering is one. With the high levels of regulation involved, including in the supply chains and standardized hardware, it's not easy for any single company to make the jump to metric on their own. Construction seems like another that will be hard to switch, especially since you still have to support maintenance on existing buildings. We're going to need 2x4s, 3/4" water supply lines, and 4"x10" air vents for a while. In fact, talking to a German friend of mine, even Germany still uses inch based measurements for plumbing for backwards compatibility. But I suspect that the U.S. will probably get there eventually, even if it takes a while. Americans are comfortable enough with metric in our lives where it does exist, so there's little incentive to switch those measurements back to USCS. And there is at least some incentive for international commerce and compatibility to switch to metric in the holdouts. In other words, I only see future changes going in one direction – from USCS to metric. So, like I said, it may take a while, but I suspect the eventual end state is complete metrification (or, at least as complete as European countries are today*). *In addition to my friend's comment about Germany using inches for plumbing, there are plenty of not actual metric units that get used in otherwise metric countries, especially when time is involved in those units – things like km/hr (instead of m/s) or kWh (instead of Joules).

When and how were you first introduced to the concepts of intelligent design and creationism? What was your initial reaction to these ideas? I actually can pinpoint this, because I was (thankfully) raised in a reasonably well educated and scientifically literate family, while going to a mainstream Catholic church that didn't really discuss issues of basic science, so evolution was just taken for granted for pretty much all of my childhood. If you want to put it in a less positive light, you might say I was a bit sheltered. My very first inkling that there were such people came in my high school biology class. We were getting ready to start the unit on evolution, when the kid sitting next to me leaned over to ask if I actually believed in evolution. I was taken a bit off guard. That's kind of like asking if you actually believe the world is a globe. But of course, I answered yes. He responded that he didn't, because there were "too many holes" (and yes, I still remember those exact words, because it really was surprising for me at the time to hear someone doubt accepted mainstream science). Anyway, we didn't really discuss it again after that. I just assumed he hadn't watched as many nature documentaries as I had, and that after everything we learned in class and how obvious evolution seemed, surely all his 'holes' must have been filled in. Fast forward several more years to my first job out of college. This was a white collar office job full of other college educated professionals. Around the water cooler one day, one guy mentioned that he thought the Earth was only a few thousand years old. A few of us started laughing thinking that he was joking, because we'd never heard anybody say anything that outlandish about the age of the Earth before. But no, he informed us. He was quite sincere, and there were actually a lot of other folks who believed the same thing he did. He told us to go look up "young Earth" on the Internet (this was back in the early 2000s, so Internet was a thing by then, if not quite as mature as today). So during my lunch break that day, I did. And I was quite surprised at the extent of information I found about Young Earth Creationism. But I still didn't dig too deep, just yet. I thought of the belief as a bit eccentric, kind of like folks who believed they could invent perpetual motion machines, but I didn't comprehend just how widespread it was. Less than a year later, I moved down to a small town in Texas for a new job. As you might expect, creationism was quite a bit more prominent there than inside the D.C. beltway. This was also around the time that Intelligent Design was hitting its peak popularity, with the landmark Kitzmiller decision set to take place in 2005. That's when I really began to pay attention and look into the statistics. And I must say, I really was shocked that nearly half of Americans rejected evolution in favor of creationism. ABOVE: A slim majority of Americans accept evolution (33% + 22%), and the numbers are slowly improving, but the number who reject evolution is still shockingly high SOURCE: Evolution, Creationism, Intelligent Design So, my first minor introductions to creationism came in my high school biology class, and then water cooler talk at my first real job, but it was the move to Texas coinciding with the rising popularity of Intelligent Design that truly got me caught up in the evolution vs. creationism culture wars. And given the religious side of the debate, it also prompted me to dig deeper into my own religious beliefs, which is actually one of the early factors that set me on the path to atheism (though certainly not the only one). Anyway, I really do find evolution quite fascinating, and I'm not sure I would have delved into it quite as deeply if not for the religious controversy. So I suppose that in a way, I have creationists to thank for motivating me to learn as much about evolution as I have (and further, for helping to nudge me towards atheism, which as I’ve said before here on Quora, I find much more fulfilling than Christianity).

If tiktaalik evolved into acanthostega, why are there no intermediary forms? Why are there no intermediary forms between any two creatures that one evolved from? This reminds me of an old joke. A creationist complains to a scientist about a gap in the fossil record between an ancient animal and a modern one. The scientist gets lucky and finds a transitional form intermediate between the two. But the creationist just replies, 'Well now you've made the problem even worse. Instead of only one gap, now you have two.' Tiktaalik was only discovered in 2004. At the time, it was heralded as a near-perfect transitional form between fish like Panderichthyes and Eushthenopteron and early tetrapods like Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, and even acquired the nickname of being a 'fishibian'. It seems it didn't take long for creationists to now see two gaps instead of just one. But to actually answer the question, the reason is because fossils are quite rare. When most organisms die, their remains are completely consumed by scavengers and decomposers. It takes a very unique and unlikely set of circumstances to preserve their remains and go through the fossilization process. And then it takes another fortuitous set of circumstances for those fossils to be exposed through erosion, and then found before erosion carries on further and destroys them completely. The fossils we've found only represent a small subset of all the life that has ever existed on this planet. Just for perspective, consider the non-bird dinosaurs. We've only found something like 700 – 1000 non-bird dinosaurs species from their entire 165 million year history. In comparison, there are 6500 named mammal species just in the present, not counting unnamed living species, or the many, many species that have existed in the past and are now extinct. So we know that the actual number of dinosaur species over that entire 165 million year history must have been orders of magnitude higher than the mere 1000 species we've found so far. And it's the same for other groups of organisms. We know that the fossil record is largely incomplete, especially the fossils we've found so far. Some transitions are extremely well documented (like older apes to modern humans). Some remain pretty much entirely undiscovered (like non-flying animals to pterosaurs). But most fall somewhere in between (like fish to tetrapods). As researchers make more and more discoveries, they continue to fill in the gaps in our understanding. And for the time being, at least, this process shows no signs of slowing down. But even though we'll probably never know all of the details, everything we have found points squarely to natural evolutionary processes. Just as a side note, given how incomplete the fossil record is, it's very unlikely that we've found direct ancestor to descendant relationships in most cases. The transitional forms are more like cousins of the actual ancestors. In some cases, we know that certain fossils can't be ancestors because of the timeframes, but that instead they've preserved certain ancestral conditions.
