WWII two boomers had 4 engines and could get back on 2 or even 1 engine. Why don’t commercial passenger aircraft have 4 engines for increased safety? Because while 4 engines provide more redundancy, they also provide more opportunities for things to break. Plus, when designing any mechanical system, there's no such thing as 100% perfectly reliable, so you have to balance how reliable is reliable enough vs. other factors like cost and maintenance. Commercial airliners have settled on a safety standard commonly referred to by the shorthand of 10^-9, or to spell it out a bit more, a risk of less than 1 catastrophic failure for every billion flight hours. That's an extremely safe standard requiring very rigorous design, analysis, testing, and tightly controlled manufacturing processes. And, to put it bluntly, there's little incentive to exceed that standard, especially if your competitors aren't, because exceeding that standard will compromise other aspects of the product. I mean, if you're going to ask about installing 4 engines instead of 2, then why not 6, or 8, or 10? Each increase would provide even more redundancy. The answer comes down to reliability and maintenance. Modern engines have roughly equivalent reliability from one model to the next. So, if you install 4 engines instead of 2, it means you'll have reliability issues twice as often, grounding the aircraft for engine related maintenance twice as often. Installing 6 engines would lead to even more maintenance downtime. And of course, it gets worse and worse the more engines you install. While more engines would provide more redundancy, the airlines would be losing money because of that extra downtime for maintenance. So it comes down to the question of how safe is safe enough? And for commercial airliners, the agreed upon value is 10^-9, which is achievable with 2 engines. It's also worth noting that piston engines are nowhere near as reliable as gas turbine engines. While a gas turbine engine can acheive 10^-9 safety with just 2 engines, you couldn't with just 2 piston engines. That's part of the reason why older, piston powered airliners had more engines. Finally, add in the fact that airliners can still glide even with a loss of all engines. Perhaps the most famous example of this is the Gimli Glider. Due to a mixup in refueling, the aircraft (a Boeing 767) ran out of fuel at 41k ft, and then proceeded to glide to an emergency landing, with no serious injuries, and only minor damage to the aircraft that was subsequently repaired and put back into service. (As a side note, this is part of the mitigation for single engine piston planes, which have no redundancy and much less reliability than gas turbine engines – the fact that they can glide to an emergency landing.) When balancing safety vs. other parameters like cost, performance, and maintenance, the agreed upon standard for commercial airliners is 10^-9 safety. And with the reliability of modern gas turbine engines, you only need 2 engines to achieve that. More engines would compromise other aspects of the design.

Do atheists believe Jesus was a person but no God? Yeah, sure. Probably. I know that there are a decent number of atheists who doubt that Jesus was a real person and think he was probably entirely legendary. But, while I don't think there's enough evidence to say anything conclusive, I do think it's more likely than not that he did exist. For one, it's a rather mundane claim. Charismatic leaders starting religious cults are a dime a dozen throughout history. We've got plenty in modern times and recent history, like Joseph Smith, L. Ron Hubbard, Jim Jones, David Koresh, Marshall Applewhite, Sun Myung Moon, Sathya Sai Babe, etc. Plenty even have stories of miracles they've performed. So the claim that a guy named Jesus (or the ancient equivalent of that name) founded a cult around 2000 years ago is not an extraordinary claim requiring extraordinary evidence. For another, unlike other mythical characters like Romulus and Remus, Robin Hood, or King Arthur, we've got Jesus pinpointed a lot more closely. Especially with the authentic letters of Paul, we've got a guy writing about this cult within living memory of Jesus, claiming to interact with folks who knew Jesus personally. We've also got the Gospels and a few extra-Biblical references from a few years later. And while the Gospels have plenty of problems around just how historically accurate they might be, it still seems reasonable that they'd be based on a real person, especially considering 'difficulties' that make more sense in light of trying to accommodate known details about a real person (the Nativity, Jesus's baptism, and the crucifixion itself). Sure, there's no eye witness or contemporary evidence, but how much of this type of evidence would you expect? If Jesus and his followers were illiterate peasants, they wouldn't have been writing much of anything themselves, so you wouldn't start to get things like Paul's letters or the Gospels until the popularity of the cult spread to more educated folks. And while some folks protest the lack of Roman records for things like the crucifixion, the fact is that we just don't have that many surviving records of anything like that from ancient Rome. Such records were written on perishable materials, so unless someone made an effort to save them, they didn't survive. We don't actually have records of any specific crucifixions from Rome, let alone Jesus's. So yeah. I think it's more likely than not that Jesus was a real cult leader 2000 years ago. As I already said, such cult leaders aren't exactly rare. The interesting thing about this cult is the way it struck a chord with so many people and rose in prominence. But that’s bound to happen from time to time, such as with later religions like Islam, Mormons, etc. For much more detail on the historicity of Jesus, here's one of the best answers I've ever come across on Quora. Is baldness a survival benefit, in the sense of Darwin's evolutionary theory of "The Survival of the Fittest"? How is baldness adventagous for survival? Meh. Who knows? Stephen J. Gould and Richard C. Lewontin wrote a seminal article cautioning against ultra-adaptationist thinking all the way back in 1979: Here's a good excerpt from the paper: We fault the adaptationist programme for its failure to distinguish current utility from reasons for origin (male tyrannosaurs may have used their diminutive front legs to titillate female partners, but this will not explain why they got so small); for its unwillingness to consider alternatives to adaptive stories; for its reliance upon plausibility alone as a criterion for accepting speculative tales; and for its failure to consider adequately such competing themes as random fixation of alleles, production of non-adaptive structures by developmental correlation with selected features (allometry, pleiotropy, material compensation, mechanically forced correlation), the separability of adaptation and selection, multiple adaptive peaks, and current utility as an epiphenomenon of non-adaptive structures. The moral is, before you try to invent just-so stories about the evolutionary advantage of a trait, you have to demonstrate that it was positively selected for in the first place. It might very well just be the result of random drift, with no real effect on fitness. A different, more recent, article by Larry Moran, On the importance of random genetic drift in modern evolutionary theory, contained these examples: Take a favorite example of Richard Lewontin who points to the fact that the African rhinoceros has two horns while the Indian rino has only one? Is this an example of natural selection? Are two horns better than one in Africa or is the null hypothesis just as likely? What about the difference between red pine, with two needles per cluster, and white pine, with five? Are those adaptations or are they just due to neutral alleles that have become fixed in the two species? Is it possible that the genes that lead to baldness have some benefit? Sure. Maybe baldness itself is attractive to some women and so affected by sexual selection. Maybe the genes that lead to baldness have other effects that are beneficial. But this type of speculation is turning into the just-so stories that Gould and Lewontin warned against. Not every feature that we've evolved was necessarily down to natural selection. Random chance plays its role, as well. I did find one fairly reasonable article that described a study showing that bald-headed men are "consistently rated as more intelligent, influential, knowledgeable, well-educated, high social status, honest and helpful – traits collectively known as social maturity." So maybe there is something to that. But it's still pretty speculative at this point.

WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc? I think you might want to consider what travel was like just a century ago before calling the present state a nightmare. I wrote an answer once about travel in the 1800s and early 1900s (Jeff Lewis's answer to Before the industrial revolution when there were no cars or planes how did people travel and how far would they typically go?). A 30 mile trip would have been an all day affair back then. Now I can do that in around half an hour. It took Wilbur Wright a week to travel from Dayton, Ohio to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Google tells me I could make that drive in a little over 10 hrs, which is within reason for a single long day. Automobiles and the Interstate Highway System (or equivalent freeways in other countries) make relatively high speed long distance travel accessible to common people. As far as common sci-fi tropes like flying cars and holographic movies, you can't invent something physically impossible. As far as we know, there's no way to create levitating vehicles, except by already understood physics like magnets, which limits your altitude to something like a maglev train, or aerodynamics, which is basically just an aircraft, and we already have those. You're never going to see something like the cars in Blade Runner that just seem to float in midair with no visibile means of propulsion. Of course, there's more than one use of the term, flying car. If you mean an aircraft with folding wings or a folding rotor, people have already built prototypes of those. The big issue is that the compromises make them subpar aircraft and subpar ground transportation – the worst of both worlds. If you mean a dedicated aircraft that doesn't drive on the road, the issue comes down to physics and hover efficiency. Helicopters look the way they do for a reason. And even the new batch of eVTOL aircraft still have a large amount of total area for their lifting devices to have any type of reasonable efficiency. ABOVE: Various eVTOL Concepts – I don't think this is what most people think of when they hear the term 'flying car'. SOURCE: eVTOL is Almost Here: What About Pilot Training? The way holograms are portrayed in movies is somewhere between very, very difficult to impossible. Keep in mind that what we see is light heading towards our eyes coming from specific locations in space. You can't just make light originate from points in space from nothing. You need something to reflect it off of, or some medium that you can make glow at certain points to generate that light. Here's one of the approaches I've seen that comes closest to what people think of as sci-fi holograms, but just imagine the engineering difficulty of scaling this up to something that could generate an entire full color screen, without the particles interfering with each other, and with opacity (instead of just see through 'wireframes'). And other than the gee whiz factor, how useful would it even be? We've already got the ability to make 3D movies, and they only come and go as brief fads. People seem perfectly content with regular movies. And movie makers use that medium to frame shots and show things from specific perspectives. Horror movies would lose their jumps scares if you had a holographic representation of the entire scene and could see the monster hiding behind the bushes. So yeah, within our lifetimes, we probably are limited to only incremental improvements beyond our current technology. But our current technology is anything but a nightmare. It really is pretty amazing when you stop and think about it, and would have seemed like a technological marvel to people from just a century ago.

If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? In American English, 'burger' on its own most certainly refers to a ground beef patty on a bun. You can stretch the definition a bit by adding a description of some other ingredient besides beef, such as a chicken burger or a veggie burger, but the implication is that it's still a ground food of some sort formed into a patty. For example, this is a chicken burger. Note the ground chicken formed into a patty: ABOVE SOURCE: Natasha's Chicken Burgers While this, since it contains a whole piece of chicken that's been breaded and fried, is a chicken sandwich: ABOVE SOURCE: The OG Chick-Fil-A Sandwich Where you can run into a bit of a gray area is a ground beef patty that's not on a bun. If you put the patty in between two slices of grilled bread with cheese, then it's a patty melt. And then it's just a question of semantics as to whether or not you think a patty melt is a type of burger or something separate. The article I copied that image from does refer to it as a specific type of burger, and I tend to agree since the defining feature of a hamburger (with it’s origins from a Hamburg steak) is the ground beef patty. ABOVE SOURCE: This Is Why Whataburger Patty Melts Are So Delicious - Mashed Yes, I know that in some other countries, practically anything on a bun is referred to as a burger. I was a bit surprised (and relieved) one time going to a get together with my German friends, when they said they were going to make chicken burgers, but they were actually making what I would call chicken sandwiches. So to answer your question, in American English, the boundary between a burger and other sandwiches is using a ground meat (or veggie) patty. No patty – no burger.

Why did it take until the 1900s before flying was invented, when the kite was invented in the 5th century? Engines. Although it might seem primitive by today's standards, here's the engine that powered the Wright Brothers' first plane, designed and built by their mechanic, Charlie Taylor. ABOVE SOURCE: 1903 Wright Engine That engine weighed 180 lbs and put out 12 horsepower. Again, that might not seem like much compared to the hugely powerful engines we have today, but horsepower really is roughly equivalent to what a horse can manage continuously (though they can go much higher for short bursts of a few seconds), so that 180 lb engine is basically doing the work of 12 horses. That's a lot. Steam engines probably could have gotten there. In fact, some of the earliest experiments with unmanned flying machines did use steam engines. And more modern steam engines have had decent power to weight ratios. ABOVE: The steam powered, unmanned Aerodrome No. 5 in flight in 1896. SOURCE: This Odd Early Flying Machine Made History but Didn't Have the Right Stuff Spruce and fabric are old technologies, so people could have built the frames and wings of aircraft for millennia. But prior to steam engines and internal combustion engines, people simply didn't have a power source with enough power at a light enough weight to enable flying machines.

How is it possible that every little detail required for life and the human species to exist on Earth just happened to happen naturally? There's probably somewhere on the order of 100 billion planets in the Milky Way galaxy, with all types of varying conditions. Just by chance, some of those planets will be conducive to life, while others won't. But guess where the intelligent life is going to be, wondering why their planets just so happen to be so well suited for their evolution. Just say that "every little detail required for life and the human species to exist" on a planet is a one in a million chance. With 100 billion planets, that still means 100,000 planets in our galaxy with those conditions. Even if it's a one in a billion chance, that's still 100 such planets. We don't yet know enough about planets outside our own solar system to say how rare it is for such conditions to exist. But even if it is extremely rare, it just stands to reason that the organisms pondering such things will be on the life supporting planets. And of course, we evolved to fit our planet, not the other way around. If other planets harbor life but with slightly different conditions, that life will almost certainly follow a different evolutionary path, producing creatures that don't resemble us humans. Also, this is an extremely self-centered question. You might as well ask how Earth is so conducive to tapeworms, or mushrooms, or oak trees. I rather like humans myself, but we're not the end-all, be-all of life on this planet. Heck, by biomass, the Earth really is a planet optimized for microbes, with us multicellular creatures just adding a bit of variety to the fringes.

What makes Google Maps superior to Apple Maps? One reason – north up maps. Maybe I'm just old fashioned from the old days of using paper maps*. But I really, really, really prefer maps to always be oriented as north up when I'm driving. I know it might not be the most intuitive when you need to make split second decisions. But in the long run, it gives you a much better perspective and sense of orientation. Especially when you're in an area where you might be spending some time and not just driving through once, it really helps you learn the area. I have a sense of the actual cardinal direction I'm heading, not just 'straight ahead'. I can see where neighborhoods lie in relation to each other. I can build up a mental map that corresponds to the map I see on the screen. In contrast, the maps that are constantly rotating to align with your direction of travel just completely destroy that sense of awareness and perspective. When I spent a few months in El Paso a couple years ago, I learned my way around much quicker thanks to Google Maps always keeping the map with north up. Otherwise, despite an ignominious beginning**, Apple Maps has grown into a decent app. It even seems to do better than Google Maps at some things, like telling you which lane to be in, and giving you more than one next step at a time. But until Apple decides to put in an option for users to keep the map oriented as north up even in guidance mode, I'm simply not going to use it. *I remember back when I was a kid, on road trip vacations, or when we first moved from Pennsylvania to Maryland, and I'd sit in the back seat of the car following along on a map to see where we were. Maybe it was all those years of practice that helps me follow along on north up maps, when so many other folks I know seem to get confused by it. **If you look at the other answers to this question, the ones trashing Apple Maps tend to be several years old. It really is a decent app, now, minus that one, monumental shortcoming.

Why do they still teach evolution in schools if it's just a theory? I see you've already received 28 prior answers to this question, but just to reiterate... Scientific theories and scientific laws are completely different things. Theories are broad frameworks, while laws are concepts that can be expressed in a single formula or short statement. To go with a non-controversial example, think about Newton's 3 Laws of Motion: ABOVE SOURCE: Newton's Laws of Motion Note how simple and short each individual law is. But these laws are a small part of the broader theory of Classical Mechanics. Classical Mechanics is so broad that there are entire textbooks devoted to the theory. ABOVE SOURCE: Amazon, but I'm not going to link to it to be on the safe side regarding spam Evolution is the same way. The high level theory is known as the Modern Synthesis, or perhaps the Extended or Integrated Synthesis, depending on who you're talking to. This high level theory is itself composed of many other theories, laws, and principles, such as Gause’s Law, Bergmann's rule, or Dollo's law of irreversibility. Just like Newton's Laws, these laws within evolutionary theory are short, pithy statements or formulas to explain a concept, and not on the same broad explanatory level as an entire theory. ABOVE SOURCE: reddit So there you have it. Creationists have been claiming the imminent demise of science for nigh on two centuries, now, and I don't expect them to stop any time soon. They're the boy who cried wolf, but who then got their kids, grandkids, and great-grandkids to carry on crying wolf long after everyone else quit paying attention to them. Do evolutionary biologists typically hold atheistic beliefs due to their understanding of human evolution? To a degree, yes. It's hard to find recent polling data on precisely this question, but there is enough related data to give a good impression. First, here's a poll on scientists’ belief in a higher power. It's from 2009, which is 15 years ago, and quite a decent time considering how quickly U.S. religious demographics have changed over the past two decades. It also just looks at scientists as a group, rather than looking at biologists in particular. However, it's still informative: ABOVE SOURCE: Scientists and Belief As you can see, only 33% of scientists believed in the capital G God, while another 18% believed in a more vague "universal spirit or higher power". On the other end, 41% didn't believe in either – a much, much higher percentage than the general public. The survey doesn't get into distinctions between atheists, agnostics, or other terms, but for the sake of this question, we'll count those 41% as some level of "atheistic beliefs". While I admittedly didn't do exhaustive searching for this, the polls I did find that broke down the responses by type of scientist were more limited to elite scientific societies such as the National Academy of Sciences or the Royal Society, rather than all practicing scientists. A correspondence to Nature from 1998, Leading scientists still reject God, polled the National Academy of Sciences and had this to say: Biological scientists had the lowest rate of belief (5.5% in God, 7.1% in immortality), with physicists and astronomers slightly higher (7.5% in God, 7.5% in immortality). The correspondence had a related figure, though unfortunately not breaking it down by field of study: ABOVE SOURCE: Table 1 Comparison of survey answers among “greater” scientists Another study, Eminent scientists reject the supernatural, surveyed the Royal Society, with similar findings, and I'll throw in results about 'consciousness surviving' as a bonus (note that the y-axis is number of respondents, not percentages): ABOVE SOURCE: Eminent scientists reject the supernatural: a survey of the Fellows of the Royal Society - Evolution: Education and Outreach Finally, let me just highlight the general shift of religious beliefs among the U.S. public over the past two decades: ABOVE SOURCE: In U.S., roughly three-in-ten adults now religiously unaffiliated Keep in mind that 'No religion' doesn't necessarily mean atheist. There are plenty of folks who are 'spiritual but not religious' who fall into that category, such that actual self-professed atheists and agnostics are only a fraction of that group. But it's still a pretty clear trend of Americans shedding faith in traditional religions. So, putting all that together, I think we can confidently say that disbelief in God or a higher power is much more prevalent among scientists than the general public, and becomes even more pronounced as you move up the ranks to more elite scientists. Also, I think we can say that biologists are even more likely to be non-believers than those in the physical sciences. As to the specific question asked here, whether "biologists typically hold atheistic beliefs", if I had to guess, I'd say probably. It was already pretty close back in 2009, and I'd guess that given the overall shift since then, that by now, the majority of biologists probably hold “atheistic beliefs”. Though whether they'd self-identify as atheists, agnostics, or something else is a bit of a different question.

Why should childless Americans pay for other people's kids to attend school? For Atheists, who is Jesus to you, given historical evidence of his existence? Which Jesus are we talking about? The Jesus of the Gospels, or the historical Jesus without all the myth and legend tacked on? By way of example, consider Saint Nicholas vs. Santa Claus. Santa Claus may be based on a real, historical Saint Nicholas, but the legend has diverged so far from reality in all that time, that the characters contain very little in common. What's more, we don't actually know all that much about the real Saint Nicholas, so it's tough to say too much about him. That's the same way it is for the historical Jesus vs. the Gospel Jesus. The historical Jesus probably existed, but there's just very little in the way of reliable evidence on what he might have been like. Paul's authentic letters are some of the earliest mentions we have of Jesus, but they don't contain much in the way of biographical details. The Gospels are much more detailed, but also come from decades later, and were almost certainly second hand accounts spread by word of mouth before educated Christians finally committed them to paper. Considering how quickly urban legends can pop up in the modern day, and how often we see misattributed quotes (Mark Twain didn't say nearly so much as the Internet memes claim he did), a decades long gap is a lot of time for the legends around Jesus to grow and morph. So it's really tough to say much of anything about the historical Jesus – whether he was an honest preacher whose image got embellished over the years, a conman who intentionally mislead people with lies and sleight of hand tricks to build a reputation as a miracle worker, a bit of a crazy religious zealot who might have believed a lot of what he said, or just about anything else you can imagine. We've got plenty of modern day religious figures as examples for any of those scenarios. As far as the more legendary Jesus of the Gospels, as I've said before, my opinion is a bit mixed. Everyone is plenty familiar with the good things he said (feed the poor, love your neighbor, don't judge others, etc.), so there's no need for me to repeat all that here. But he also had plenty of more troubling teachings. Since I've already written about this before (Jeff Lewis's answer to Being an atheist, I know you do not believe in God, but do you see Jesus (the character) as being a good role model? Why?), I'm going to quote that here: But let's not forget who the historical Jesus was – a religious extremist and a cult leader. He supposedly told his followers things like, "Whoever is not with me is against me," and "Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple." If a Jim Jones, David Koresh, or L. Ron Hubbard were to say such things we'd call them out as gigantic red flags. Just because Christianity went on to become a major religion doesn't mean it was okay when (if) Jesus said those things in the first place. Although Christians were quick to rationalize/accommodate Jesus's failed prophecies, he himself seemed to believe that the coming age of the Son of Man was imminent, "Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." That, and his belief that God would take care of people with enough faith, led to several teachings that are rather irresponsible if you actually have to plan for the future. "Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What will we eat?’ or ‘What will we drink?’ or ‘What will we wear?’ For it is the Gentiles who strive for all these things; and indeed your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things." Or his admonition to the rich young man, "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me." At times, Jesus also had a bit of a black & white way of looking at the world that lacked subtlety or nuance. One that's bothered me for a while is the way he equated temptation to actually acting on it. Consider his teaching on lust, "But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart." Seriously, ask any married person if they'd be as upset at their spouse for a momentary feeling of lust, or actually committing adultery. This type of teaching just sets people up for failure. Instead of framing it as a positive that someone was able to overcome their temptations, it berates people for having normal, natural emotions in the first place. [Going even further, you could frame that as adultery being no worse than lust, so if you've already lusted after somebody, you're not doing anything worse by actually carrying trough with action.] Then there's the whole episode with the money changers in the temple, which very well may have been the incident that led to his crucifixion. Now, it's one thing to have strong principles and to stand up for them. But it's another thing altogether to go onto somebody else's property to cause a major disturbance, vandalize the premises, and assault the people there. I mean, I can think of one church in particular here in my own town that I don't like, but I'm not going to show up there on a Sunday morning, smash up their altar, and start chasing people out of the pews. That's not how mature, sensible people handle disagreements. Finally, this last one may be a little unfair to the historical Jesus, since it comes from one of the stories that arose after his death, but I've always hated the doubting Thomas story. "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe." No, no, no. It is not a virtue to believe things without evidence. It's this type of gullibility and naivety that leads people to give all their money to Nigerian princesses. Critical thinking and skepticism (not to be confused with cynicism) are skillsets that should be nurtured and celebrated, not discouraged. So, it's tough to say anything about the historical Jesus, because we just don't have much reliable evidence to know what he was really like. The Jesus of the Gospels was a mixed bag, with some good teachings, but plenty of troubling ones. Related:

Should creationism be taught in public schools as an alternative to evolution, given its religious roots, or does doing so infringe upon the separation of church and state? There are two aspects of this answer. First, of course teaching creationism in public schools violates the separation of church and state in the U.S. This has repeatedly been the interpretation of courts, from Epperson v. Arkansas back in 1968 to the more recent Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District in 2005 (Ten Major Court Cases about Evolution and Creationism). But that's only a legal technicality. What if we didn't have the First Amendment, or lived in a different country that didn't enshrine the separation of church and state? Well, then we have the much more fundamental issue that creationism is wrong. I don't think many people realize that creationism was the dominant scientific paradigm prior to Darwin. Some naturalists may have toyed with ideas of 'transmutation', but they were largely seen as fringe eccentrics. At best, some naturalists were more in line with certain modern day creationists who concede evolution within 'kinds', but not universal common descent. It was the plausible theory and especially the evidence that Darwin presented in The Origin that basically convinced the scientific community practically overnight to accept evolution over creationism. In other words, those naturalists didn't reject creationism because they were a priori opposed to it, but because the evidence conclusively favored evolution over creationism. And in the 150+ years since then, the evidence for evolution has only grown even more overwhelming. So yes, teaching creationism in public schools in the U.S. would violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. But even more importantly, creationism is factually incorrect and not good science, so why would you want to teach it to our children in the first place?

Why do people have a problem with Christianity so much? Or is it because they think it might/could be the true religion? As an atheist, I don't think any religions are true. But living in the U.S., our country is so saturated with Christianity that Christianity is the religion that affects me by far the most. Here, for example, are the results from a fairly recent poll on the religious makeup in the U.S.: ABOVE SOURCE: The Largest Survey Ever Conducted of American Religious and Denominational Identity: 14 Major Findings from a Landmark Study Note that all the blue and green slices are Christians. Purple and grey are unaffiliated or people who didn't respond. Only those small orange slices are non-Christian religions (and arguably, Jehovah's Witnesses should have been included with the Christians instead). None of those other religions make up a large enough percentage of the population to have much influence. Anecdotally, I've never had a Buddhist come knocking on my door to preach their scriptures. I've never found Muslim tracts hidden in books at the bookstore. I haven't seen Hindus shouting with a megaphone on a street corner when I was just trying to get into the Stars game. But I've experienced all of those, and more, from Christians. And that's not even getting into the political influence of those Christians. Notice how nearly a quarter of those folks in the above graph were Unaffiliated, and it's actually closer to 30% in more recent surveys (How U.S. religious composition has changed in recent decades). But do you know what the Congress and Senate look like? ABOVE SOURCE: Faith on the Hill In the House, nobody specifically identified as unaffiliated, atheist, or agnostic. Though a whopping 1 person did identify as Humanist, and 3.7% responded with "Don't know/Refused to answer". In the Senate, there was 1 senator who identified as unaffiliated, and a further 4 who went with the "Don't know/Refused to answer". So in a nation where around 30% of the population is religiously unaffiliated, and only around 2/3 are Christians, 88% of House members are Christian, while 85% of Senators are. Now, I know that plenty of Christians are perfectly capable of separating their religious beliefs from secular concerns, and do respect the First Amendment's separation of church and state, and that it's not all Christians trying to enforce religiously based laws. How do atheists respond to the saying "everything happens for a reason" after experiencing something negative? Is there a counter argument from an atheist perspective? Why do we need a counter argument? You're the one with the saying with troubling implications for reality – that we're all at the mercy of some cosmic puppeteer putting us through the ringer for unfathomable reasons beyond our control. I mean, the common expression is to 'accept your fate', not 'embrace' it or 'rejoice in' it. There's a sense of resignation, of submitting to the biggest bully on the block. So I guess the simplest atheist 'counter argument' is that no, the universe isn't quite that bad. Bad things beyond our control may still happen, but at least it's not some entity toying with us on purpose. However, if you want some more common expressions, there are plenty. One of my favorites that I use quite often is, 'It is what it is.' If you want to sound a bit fancier using a foreign language, you could say 'Que será, será.' Or if you want to go a little more low brow, you can go with the old standby, 'Shit happens.' All of these have a similar intent behind them, that we live in a universe where many things will happen beyond our control. It does no good to dwell on why or what if*, because that still won't change it. Our best course of action is to accept those things, and then do the only thing we can do, control how we react and what actions we ourselves take going forward. *Of course, I don't mean to ignore causes altogether if understanding those causes can help inform your actions in the future. I mean 'why' and 'what if' in a more metaphysical sense. For example, understanding the causes of an airplane accident can drive regulations, retrofits, or training to avoid future accidents. But there's nothing we can do to change accidents that have already happened.

How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight? Exercise is very important for overall fitness and health, but not so much for losing weight. And even the benefits it does have for weight loss are a case of diminishing returns. In other words, if you exercise an hour a week, that is better for weight loss than sitting around doing nothing. But exercising for two hours a week isn't going to double the weight loss benefit. Your body has a certain basal metabolic rate that it needs simply for surviving. Even if you do nothing but sit at a desk all day, you know you still need to eat. And this basal metabolic rate is actually the biggest energy expenditure for most of us, accounting for something like 60–80% of our calories. ABOVE: Components of total energy expenditure for an average young adult woman and man. SOURCE: Why you shouldn't exercise to lose weight, explained with 60+ studies But as we start doing more physical activity, our body compensates. In order to save energy to help keep our food requirements down (because historically, starving was a much bigger danger than obesity), our body reduces the energy put into the basal metabolic rate. ABOVE: The body adapts to increased physical activity by reducing energy spent on other physiological activities. SOURCE: Why you shouldn't exercise to lose weight, explained with 60+ studies As you can see in the figure above, going from a sedentary lifestyle to a moderate amount of exercise does substantially increase your total energy expenditure. But as you keep pushing the physical activity higher and higher, the compensation from our body causes the total energy expenditure to somewhat level off. Sure, if you're an elite athlete doing tons of training, you'll need more calories than most of us. But most of us aren't elite athletes. And the calorie counters on your Fitbit or treadmill aren't all that accurate to begin with, and don't take into account any drop off in your basal metabolic rate. So just because your Fitbit says you burned a certain amount of additional calories by tacking on another exercise, don't think that that justifies you consuming that many more calories. The Fitbit is likely wrong. So, exercise for your health and fitness. It really is the right thing to do. But when it comes to losing weight, pay attention to what you're eating, and eat less.

What scientific fact, study, or research do you base your claim of God’s non-existence? Not one of you non-believers has provided a more suitable answer greater than lack of proof or evidence. Believer's faith is in the Bible. What's yours based in? There's a big difference between the capital G God of the Bible, and a more generic lower case g god or higher power. The generic higher power is more difficult to 'disprove', and it's in this sense that many atheists admit there's still a small possibility of a god existing. But the capital G God of the Bible? Well, we've got the Bible itself to look at, along with archaeology. I've written about such things many times on Quora, and it would be easy to turn this into a Gish Gallop. In fact, I've already written such a 'Gish Gallop' type answer, which itself includes many links to other answers and articles: The introduction to that question is as good a summary as any: In short, the Bible seems exactly like the type of collection of stories that would develop organically over generations within a bronze age to iron age culture, and nothing at all like an inerrant work inspired by an actual God. There are all types of indications and clues within the Bible itself of how it developed over the generations, including the people’s changing concept of Yahweh. The early parts in Genesis seem like just-so stories that obviously don't match history on a literal level, and later parts like Exodus and the conquest of the Holy Land don't match archaeological evidence. And on top of all that, there are some stories that are just absurd at face value. To list just one example here, I'll go with the Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions*. The Kuntillet Ajrud archaeological site dates to some time around the 8th century, B.C. It was most likely "an Israelite state-sponsored enterprise" (source: The Inscriptions of Kuntillet ‛Ajrud Through the Lens of Historical Research). Among the findings there are inscriptions and drawings mentioning El, Yahweh, Ba'al, and Yahweh's wife, Asherah. For example, one of these inscriptions (on Pithos A) includes: I have blessed you by YHWH of Samaria and to [his†] Asherata. While another (on Pithos B) includes: I have blessed you by YHWH of Teman and [his†] Asherata. ABOVE: A projection drawing of Pithos A, which includes the wording, "I have blessed you by YHWH of Samaria and to [his†] Asherata." SOURCE: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Projection-drawing-of-Pithos-A-Meshel-et-al-2012-87-Fig-524-147-Fig-65-tags_fig1_318275592 So, right off the bat, we have a depiction of Yahweh that predates the composition of much of the the Bible‡, and shows the belief that he had a wife. (And note that these weren't the only two such inscriptions from the site.) This shows that the precursor to monotheistic Judaism was a polytheistic religion, where Yahweh wasn't the only god or goddess. It's also significant that there were separate mentions of a Yahweh of Samaria and a Yahweh of Teman. At the very least, these types of localized centers of worship contradict the Biblical narrative that the worship of Yahweh had been centralized to the Temple of Jerusalem by that point. But, according to that paper I already linked to, the author believes these different Yahwehs actually represent different regional deities with "distinct cultic vessels, rituals and ceremonies". The Yahweh of Samaria was only concerned with Samaria, while the Yahweh of Teman was concerned only with Teman. And further, a certain amount of the Deuteronomistic influence§ in the Bible was trying to bring these disparate religions and customs together into a unified religion for all of Israel and Judah. As one more quick note, another inscription from the site contains what may be a version of the story of Moses and the Exodus, but, according to that same paper, with "marked differences compared to the canonical biblical story, confirming the assumption of scholars that biblical traditions developed gradually over many years." So, from the archaeological findings at Kuntillet Ajrud, we have evidence showing one of the steps in the development of Yahweh, as a local deity with a goddess for a wife, before he developed into the monotheistic God of all creation that most people are familiar with, now. We also have details showing that the Biblical narrative isn't completely trustworthy, since worship of Yahweh hadn't yet been centralized to the Temple at Jerusalem like the story claims. And as I said, that's just from one archaeological site. That other answer that I already linked to provides many, many more examples. If you don't feel like scrolling back up to the top of this answer, here's that link again for easy reference: Even More Info: If you want a really, really detailed explanation, I wrote a short book that I self-published, that you can download for free from my personal website (since it is available as a free download, I trust this isn't spam according to Quora's policies): Footnotes: * Portions of this section were adapted from a prior answer: † I included the 'his' in brackets in those quotes because some researchers think there's a possessive suffix attaching Asherat to Yahweh, while others think the suffix is actually just part of the name, Asherata. ‡ The composition of the Bible is a whole topic in itself, that I did cover in the previously linked 'Gish Gallop' answer. § That 'Deuteronomistic influence' is part of the same topic of the composition of the Bible.

Why is there a theory to evolution? Because that’s how science works. Theories are the high level frameworks we use to study things. In my own field of aerospace engineering, for example, let’s say I wanted to analyze a propeller. For a back of the envelope type analysis, I could use momentum theory. If I want to dig a little deeper, I could use blade element theory. If I want to go even further, I could use computational fluid dynamics. So, I’ve got at least three different theories I can use to analyze the same thing (with many different levels of implementation even within each of those theories). Evolution’s the same way. We know it happens, but there are different ways of looking at it and different theories you can use to study it. The over-arching high level theory is the modern synthesis or the extended synthesis, but there are sub-parts to that, many of which could be considered theories in their own right: ABOVE SOURCE: Epigenetic opportunities for Evolutionary Computation And off the top of my head, even that figure is leaving out lower level concepts like genetic drift, neutral theory, Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, etc. Basically, there are theories to evolution, because evolution is science, and science uses theories.

Why is the left so adamant in their denial that COVID-19 came from the Wuhan virology lab? It's like a chocolate flood in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Might it be from the candy factory? If you have a half hour or so, I'd really recommend reading the whole thing: I think the two pieces of evidence that I found the most convincing had to do with the original cases. They were centered around the wet market in Wuhan, not the Wuhan Institute of Virology: ABOVE SOURCE: Practically-A-Book Review: Rootclaim $100,000 Lab Leak Debate And even more specifically, the cases within the market were centered around a racoon dog vendor, an animal which is a known carrier of COVID-19: ABOVE SOURCE: Practically-A-Book Review: Rootclaim $100,000 Lab Leak Debate In fact, two years before the pandemic, a scientist who was visiting that very same market took a picture of the conditions of the racoon dogs, because he was told even back then that "This is the kind of place that has the ingredients for cross-species transmission of dangerous pathogens." ABOVE: Conditions of racoon dogs and birds in the wet market back in 2014 SOURCE: NPR IMAGE CREDIT: Eddie Holmes As that debate I linked to put it: People say it would be a surprising coincidence if a zoonotic coronavirus pandemic just so happened to start in a city with a big coronavirus research lab, and this is true. But it would be an even more surprising coincidence if a lab-leak coronavirus pandemic just so happened to first get detected at a raccoon-dog stall in a wet market! The other piece of evidence concerning the first cases has to do with the two separate early lineages of COVID-19, Lineage A and Lineage B. Another strong piece of evidence is that COVID-19 seems most likely to have evolved from a related coronavirus, BANAL-52. But BANAL-52 wasn't discovered until after the pandemic, once interest in the origins of COVID-19 had spiked and people were trying very hard to determine where it came from. Does anyone think of how to combine the Bible and science? Back a couple decades ago when I went through a crisis of faith, I had that youthful combination of naivety and arrogance to think that I could be the one to do this myself. Up until then, I had accepted both science and religion, and reconciled the discrepancies with hand-wavy explanations about trying to explain science to primitive people with no real understanding of geologic time scales or the scale of the universe. You've no doubt heard similar arguments plenty of times, such as the days in Genesis actually representing ages rather than literal 24 hour periods. However, once you start taking a closer look at Bible stories, these rationalizations don't really hold up – at least, not if you're looking for some way to keep the biblical narrative lined up with reality. I mean, according to Genesis, God didn't create the Sun until the fourth day, after the Earth, oceans, and even plants. You can't reconcile that with reality just by saying the days were supposed to represent very long ages. You can try getting even more creative with your interpretations and the symbolism, but by that point, you're really just trying to shoehorn the Bible to match reality, not interpreting it in any type of way that would be obvious without already knowing the science. I've seen others argue that you shouldn't even try to reconcile Genesis with reality, that it's not even a simplified narrative of reality, but just pure allegory (e.g. What is the Relationship Between the Creation Accounts in Genesis 1 and 2? - BioLogos). One issue with this is that it's not obvious from the Bible itself that this is the case, as evidenced by the centuries and centuries that people did take the stories seriously, and did believe that the Earth was only a few thousand years old. It was only once we learned the truth through science that people were forced to reinterprate the Bible out of necessity. And even if you want to say that the more mythical stories like Genesis are allegory, what about other parts like the conquest of the Promised Land? Those read much more like supposed history, but they're also largely inconsistent with real history. See for example, this excellent answer from Frans du Plessis: And once you do get past this preconception that the Bible has to be consistent with reality, you can recognize the actual beliefs of the culture that developed it. For example, the older books like Genesis really do seem to present a flat Earth cosmology. And once you recognize and accept that, you don't have to put yourself through cognitive dissonance trying to force the Bible to say things that the writers never intended. ABOVE CREDIT: Ben Stanhope, (Mis)interpreting Genesis: How the Creation Museum Misunderstands the Ancient Near Eastern Context of the Bible (Scarab Press: Louisville Kentucky, 2018), 88. SOURCE: Old Testament Cosmology Basically, even as somebody who started out from the position of wanting to reconcile the Bible with science, once I began looking into it in detail, I realized that the Bible really is just a collection of very human writings from an ancient society with no particularly special insights or inspiration from the divine. There's no more reason to expect scientific accuracy from the Bible than from any other ancient mythology.

If we sent a probe deep into space and it was always live streaming footage from launch, would it still have any kind of delay the further it goes out? Yes, it will still have a delay, and the delay will get longer the further away from Earth the probe gets. I think what may be confusing you is that the video signal will be continuous and seem to be in real time. If the delay is negligible at the moment the probe launches, but measurable once the probe is far away, what's going on? The answer is that the 'live' footage you're receiving from the probe is actually just a tiny, tiny bit slower than real time. Let's take the Voyager 1 probe as an example, since it's the most distant probe so far, and let's just pretend for the sake of argument that Voyager had been sending a constant live stream. Voyager 1 is so far from Earth that it takes 22.5 hours for a radio signal sent from Voyager to reach us, nearly a full day. But, Voyager 1 was launched back in 1977, just about 47 years ago. Let's just round those numbers off a bit, and say that Voyager 1 left 17,167 days ago, and that it now takes a full day for a radio signal from Voyager to reach us. What that means is that a video stream that took 17,167 days of real time on Voyager would take 17,168 days to receive back on Earth. Simply dividing those numbers, you see that the 'playback time' on Earth was 1.000058251 times longer than the 'recording time' on Voyager. A playback speed that's 1.000058251 slower than real-time is not going to be noticeable to people viewing the live stream. But it is enough to account for the increasing time delay over half a century.
